rationale: The book's closing repeats its opening formula almost word for word: God “sent His angel to show His slaves the things that must take place soon.” The two verses frame the whole revelation.

Both verses describe the revelation as delivered through an angel sent by Jesus: “I, Jesus, sent My angel to testify these things.” Revelation 22:16 restates in Jesus’ own voice the chain of transmission set out in the opening verse.

Daniel speaks of a God in heaven who “disclosed” to the king “what must happen in the last days,” and Revelation opens with what God gave “to show His slaves the things that must take place.” Daniel’s disclosure comes through a dream to a king, whereas Revelation’s comes through an angel to John.
Both verses join “the word of God” and “the testimony of Jesus” as the content of John’s witness. Revelation 1:9 gives this pairing as the reason John was on Patmos.

The martyrs under the altar were slain “because of the word of God and because of the testimony they held,” the same pairing that describes what John testified to. In Revelation 6:9 the testimony is that held by the martyrs rather than “the testimony of Jesus Christ” by name.
The opening and closing of the book both pronounce a blessing on the one who keeps “the words of the prophecy.” Revelation 22:7 joins this beatitude to the promise “I am coming quickly.”
Both verses speak of “the words of the prophecy” and close with the same reason, “for the time is near.” In Revelation 22:10 the point is that the scroll is not to be sealed.
Both pronounce a blessing on those who hear and keep: “blessed are those who hear the word of God and keep it.” Luke speaks of the word of God generally, Revelation of the words of this prophecy.
Both use the identical threefold title “the One who is and who was and who is coming.” Revelation 1:8 places it on the lips of the Lord God together with “the Alpha and the Omega” and “the Almighty.”

Revelation 1:4 mentions “the seven spirits before His throne,” and Revelation 4:5 sees “seven lamps of fire” burning “before the throne, which are the seven spirits of God.” The later vision gives the image behind the greeting’s phrase.

In the Greek wording followed here, God names Himself to Moses “the One Who Is,” the first element of Revelation’s title for God. Exodus has only this single designation; Revelation extends it with “who was and who is coming.”

The Psalm promises to make the anointed king “firstborn, high among the kings of the earth,” and Revelation calls Jesus “the firstborn of the dead and the ruler of the kings of the earth.” Revelation adds “of the dead,” applying the title to resurrection.
Both call Christ “the firstborn from the dead” (Revelation: “of the dead”). Colossians links the title to His having “first place in all things,” Revelation to His rule over “the kings of the earth.”

Both speak of deliverance from sins by Jesus’ blood: “freed us from our sins in His blood” and “the blood of Jesus His Son cleanses us from every sin.” John’s letter frames this within walking in the light and fellowship.
Both say that Christ has made His people “a kingdom” and “priests” to God. Revelation 5:10 sets this in the song to the Lamb and adds that “they shall reign upon the earth.”

At Sinai God tells Israel, “you shall be to Me a royal priesthood and a holy nation,” the background for Revelation’s “a kingdom, priests.” Exodus addresses the sons of Israel; Revelation applies the status to those freed by Christ’s blood.

Both close with an ascription of “the glory and the dominion” forever, ending in “Amen.” Peter directs it to God through Jesus Christ, while Revelation directs it to the One who loves us and freed us.

Daniel sees “one like a son of man” coming “upon the clouds of heaven,” and Revelation announces, “He is coming with the clouds.” Daniel’s figure is seen in a night vision; Revelation applies the image to a coming seen by “every eye.”

Zechariah says that they “will look toward Me” and “mourn over him,” matching Revelation’s seeing and mourning “over Him.” The Greek-based wording here reads “because they danced in mockery,” so the word “pierced” in Revelation is not found in this Zechariah text.

Both combine the coming “upon the clouds” with the statement that “all the tribes of the earth will mourn.” Matthew speaks of “the Son of Man” and “the sign” in heaven; Revelation adds “those who pierced Him.”
Both use the self-designation “I am the Alpha and the Omega.” Revelation 22:13 expands it with “the first and the last, the beginning and the end.”
Both join “Lord God” and “Almighty” with the threefold title of the One who is, was and is coming. Revelation 4:8 gives the order “who was and who is and who is coming” in the living creatures’ hymn.

God declares, “I am first, and I am after these things; apart from Me there is no God,” expressing in Isaiah what “the Alpha and the Omega” expresses with the first and last letters. Isaiah does not use the alphabet image.
Both verses identify John’s witness with “the word of God” and “the testimony of Jesus.” Revelation 1:2 describes what John testified to; 1:9 gives the same pair as the reason he was on Patmos.
Both join affliction with the kingdom: John is a partner “in the affliction and kingdom,” and Acts teaches that “through many afflictions we must enter the kingdom of God.”

The angel calls himself John’s “fellow slave” and of his “brothers who hold the testimony of Jesus,” echoing John’s description of himself as “brother and fellow partner” because of “the testimony of Jesus.”
Both describe a voice “like a trumpet” speaking to John and his coming to be “in the Spirit.” In Revelation 4:1–2 this leads to the vision of the heavenly throne.

John is “carried me away in the Spirit” to see the woman on the scarlet beast, using the same “in the Spirit” language that opens the first vision. Revelation 17:3 involves being carried to a place, which 1:10 does not mention.
John is “carried me away in the Spirit” to see the holy city Jerusalem, the same phrase that introduces the first vision. As with 17:3, the later verse adds a transport to a location.
Both are divine commands to write down a vision: “What thou seest, write” and “Write a vision clearly.” Habakkuk names a tablet; Revelation names a scroll to be sent to seven Churches.
The Lord tells Jeremiah, “Write in a book all the words I delivered to you,” a close parallel to John’s command to “write in a scroll.” Jeremiah records spoken oracles, John what he sees.
Both name the addressees as “the seven Churches,” 1:4 placing them “in Asia” and 1:11 listing the seven cities by name.
Zechariah sees a golden lampstand with “seven lamps upon it,” the background for John’s golden lampstands. Zechariah sees one lampstand bearing seven lamps, John “seven golden lampstands.”
Revelation 1:20 explains “the seven golden lampstands” as “seven Churches,” and 2:1 describes Christ as walking “in the midst of the seven golden lampstands.”
The next verse completes the scene John turned to see: “in the midst of the lampstands One like a son of man.”
Both use the description “one like a son of man.” Daniel’s figure comes upon the clouds of heaven; Revelation’s stands among the lampstands.

Daniel sees “a man clothed in fine linen” with linen “wrapped around his waist,” comparable to the figure “clothed in a robe” and “girded around the chest with a golden belt.” Daniel places the girding at the waist and does not mention gold.
The seven angels are “girded around their chests with golden belts,” the same attire described for the One like a son of man.

Daniel describes the Ancient of Days with a covering “like snow” and hair “like pure white wool,” with a throne “like a flame of fire.” Revelation applies white wool and snow to the head and hair and the flame of fire to the eyes.
Daniel’s heavenly man has “eyes like flaming torches,” comparable to “eyes like a flame of fire.”
The letter to Thyatira introduces the Son of God as having “His eyes like a flame of fire,” repeating this feature of the opening vision.
The letter to Thyatira repeats “His feet like burnished bronze” from the opening vision.

Daniel’s heavenly man has “arms and feet like flashing bronze” and speech like “the sound of an uproar,” paralleling the bronze feet and overwhelming voice. Daniel does not use the phrase “many waters.”
The Psalm speaks of “the voices of many waters” with the Lord wondrous on high, matching “the sound of many waters.” In the Psalm the waters are the sea, not the Lord’s voice itself.
The letter to Pergamum introduces Christ as “the One who hath the sharp two-edged sword,” repeating this feature of the opening vision.
The servant says God “made my mouth like a sharp sword,” the image behind the sword coming from Christ’s mouth. In Isaiah the mouth is compared to a sword; in Revelation a sword comes out of it.
At the transfiguration Jesus’ face “shone like the sun,” comparable to His appearance “like the sun shining in its strength.”
God says, “I am first, and I am after these things,” the background to “I am the first and the last.” Isaiah’s wording uses “after these things” rather than “the last.”
The letter to Smyrna introduces Christ as “the first and the last, who became dead and lived,” repeating the self-designation of 1:17 together with 1:18.
Ezekiel, seeing the likeness of the Lord’s glory, falls upon his face and hears a voice speaking, as John falls “at His feet as dead” and is spoken to. Ezekiel is not touched by a hand in this verse.
Both state that Christ died and now lives without death having power over Him: “no longer dies; death no longer rules over Him,” and “I became dead, and behold, I am living for the ages of the ages.”

Wisdom ascribes to God “authority over life and death” and the power to bring down to and up from “the gates of Hades,” comparable to Christ’s “keys of death and Hades.” Wisdom speaks of gates, Revelation of keys.
“Death and Hades” appear again as a pair when they are “thrown into the lake of fire,” showing the end of the powers whose keys Christ holds.
The command “write the things thou sawest” repeats the first commission in 1:11, “What thou seest, write in a scroll.” 1:19 adds the things that are and the things to take place after these.
The first letter introduces Christ as holding “the seven stars in His right hand” and walking among “the seven golden lampstands,” the two symbols explained in 1:20.
Revelation 1:16 is the description being explained: “He held seven stars in His right hand.”
Zechariah’s golden lampstand with “seven lamps upon it” stands behind the seven golden lampstands. Zechariah has one lampstand, and the explanation as Churches is Revelation’s own.
Both mention the seven stars in the right hand and “the seven golden lampstands”; 1:20 explains them as angels of the Churches and the Churches themselves.
The title in the letter to Ephesus repeats from the opening vision that He “held seven stars in His right hand.”

Both concern people who claim to be apostles falsely: Paul speaks of “false apostles” disguising themselves “as apostles of Christ,” and Ephesus tested “those who call themselves apostles and are not.”

Both commend testing claimants: “test the spirits to see whether they are from God,” and “thou didst test those who call themselves apostles.” John’s letter speaks of false prophets rather than false apostles.
The letter to Smyrna uses the same pattern of false self-description, “those who say that they themselves are Jews and are not,” as Ephesus’s “those who call themselves apostles and are not.”
Jesus foretells hostility “because of My name,” and the Ephesians are commended for bearing up “for My name’s sake.”
Philadelphia is commended for keeping “the word of My endurance,” the same quality of endurance tied to Christ for which Ephesus is praised.

The Lord remembers Israel’s early “love of your completion” and asks why their fathers “withdrew far from Me,” comparable to the charge “thou didst abandon thy first love.” Jeremiah addresses Israel, Revelation a Church.
Jesus warns that “the love of many will grow cold,” a decline of love comparable to the abandoned first love. Matthew ties this to increasing lawlessness, which Revelation 2:4 does not mention.
The letter to Thyatira uses the identical rebuke, “But I have this against thee.”
Both call for repentance with a conditional threat: “Therefore repent. Otherwise I am coming to thee.” At Pergamum the threat is war with the sword of His mouth; at Ephesus removal of the lampstand.
Sardis is also told to “remember,” to “repent,” and that He will come upon them, matching the sequence remember, repent and coming in the warning to Ephesus.
Revelation 1:20 explains that “the seven lampstands are seven Churches,” giving the meaning of the threat to “move thy lampstand from its place.”
The only other mention of the Nicolaitans is in the letter to Pergamum, which has “those who hold the teaching of the Nicolaitans.” Ephesus hates their works; Pergamum tolerates their teaching.
The Psalmist hates “those who hate Thee,” sharing God’s hostility toward His enemies, as Ephesus hates works “which I also hate.” Revelation speaks of hating works, the Psalm of hating people.
Genesis places “the tree of life in the midst of the garden,” the tree promised to the conqueror “in the Paradise of God.”

The book’s closing speaks of having “right to the tree of life,” fulfilling the promise to give the conqueror “to eat from the tree of life.” There the condition is washing robes rather than conquering.
The letter to Pergamum ends with the identical call to hear “what the Spirit saith to the Churches” and a promise beginning “To the one who conquereth I will give.”
The title of the letter to Smyrna repeats Christ’s words in the opening vision: “I am the first and the last” and “I became dead, and behold, I am living.”
Smyrna is the second of the seven Churches named in the commission to write to the Churches.
Both speak of “the synagogue of Satan” and of “those who say that they themselves are Jews and are not.” Revelation 3:9 adds that they “lie” and will bow before the Church in Philadelphia.
Smyrna is poor “but thou art rich,” whereas Laodicea says “I am rich” but is “poor.” The two letters reverse the same contrast of riches and poverty.
James says God chose “those poor in the world to be rich in faith,” matching the paradox “poverty—but thou art rich.”
Both promise “the crown of life” to those who remain faithful under trial: James to the man who “endures a trial,” Revelation to those who are “tested” and become “faithful until death.”
Both state that the second death has no power over the faithful: “over these the second death hath no authority,” and “shall certainly not be harmed by the second death.”
Revelation 20:14 defines the second death as “the lake of fire,” explaining what the conqueror will not be harmed by.
Revelation 21:8 also identifies the burning lake as “the second death” and lists those whose share is in it, the contrast to the conqueror’s promise.
The title repeats from the opening vision that “a sharp two-edged sword was coming out” of His mouth.
Later in the same letter Christ threatens to “wage war against them with the sword of My mouth,” applying the title given in 2:12.

Hebrews compares the word of God to a “two-edged sword” that judges; Revelation presents Christ as having “the sharp two-edged sword.” Hebrews uses the sword as a comparison, not as a feature of a vision.
Philadelphia is commended because it “didst not deny My name,” as Pergamum holds fast His name and “didst not deny My faith.”
Paul calls Stephen “Thy witness” at the time of his killing, as Antipas is “My witness, My faithful one, who was killed.”

Numbers says that the women, “according to Balaam’s word,” caused the sons of Israel to turn away at Peor, the episode behind Balaam teaching Balak to put a stumbling block “before the sons of Israel.” Numbers does not name Balak in this verse.
The charge against Thyatira names the same two sins, eating “things sacrificed to idols” and committing “sexual immorality,” attributed there to Jezebel rather than Balaam.
The Jerusalem letter requires abstaining from “things sacrificed to idols” and “sexual immorality,” the two practices condemned in the teaching of Balaam.
The only other mention of the Nicolaitans is in the letter to Ephesus, which hates “the works of the Nicolaitans.” Pergamum, by contrast, has those who hold their teaching.
The “sword of My mouth” recalls the opening vision, in which “from His mouth a sharp two-edged sword was coming out.”
In Revelation 19:15 “from His mouth cometh out a sharp sword” to strike the nations, carrying out the war with the sword of His mouth threatened here.

Isaiah’s king will “strike the earth with the word of his mouth” and slay the ungodly with the breath of his lips, the background for judgment by what comes from the mouth. Isaiah does not speak of a sword.

Isaiah promises, “He will call you your new name, which the Lord will name,” comparable to the “new name written” given to the conqueror. Isaiah addresses Zion; Revelation an individual conqueror, with the name on a white stone.
Isaiah says, “Those serving Him will be called a new name,” paralleling the promise of a new name to the conqueror.
The promise to Philadelphia also includes a new name written on the conqueror: “I will write upon him … My new name.”
The Psalm’s decree, “You are My son,” lies behind the title “the Son of God” used in this letter,. The Psalm addresses the anointed king, while Revelation uses the title of the risen Christ.
Thyatira is the fourth of the seven Churches named in the commission to write to the Churches.
Both letters begin “I know thy works” and commend “endurance,” but Ephesus has abandoned its “first love,” whereas Thyatira’s “last works are more than the first.”
Paul gives thanks that the Thessalonians’ faith is growing and their love increasing, comparable to Thyatira’s love and faith with later works exceeding the first.
Ahab took as wife “Jezebel” and served Baal, the queen whose name is given to the false prophetess at Thyatira. Kings does not call Jezebel a prophetess.
Both charges name the same two sins, “sexual immorality” and eating “things sacrificed to idols,” attributed in 2:14 to the teaching of Balaam.
Kings speaks of “the blood of all the Lord’s slaves at Jezebel’s hand,” while Revelation says Jezebel “deceiveth My slaves.” In Kings she kills the Lord’s slaves; in Revelation she leads them astray.
After the trumpet plagues the survivors “did not repent of … their sexual immorality,” the same refusal to repent of sexual immorality ascribed to Jezebel.
Wisdom says that in judging gradually God “didst give room for repentance” to those who would not change, as Christ “gave her time to repent.”
Paul speaks of God’s forbearance meant to lead to “repentance” and of an “unrepentant heart” that stores up wrath, comparable to time given and repentance refused.

Ezekiel announces punishment “of an adulteress” and says “All women will be disciplined,” comparable to judgment on Jezebel and on those committing adultery with her. Ezekiel’s penalties are stoning and the sword rather than a bed and affliction.
God gathers against the unfaithful city “all your lovers” and exacts “the retribution of an adulteress,” paralleling judgment falling on the adulteress and her partners.
The kings who “committed sexual immorality” with Babylon will weep and mourn over her, comparable to the great affliction for those committing adultery with Jezebel.

The Lord says, “I, the Lord, examine hearts and test kidneys, to give each according to his ways,” combining both elements of Revelation 2:23: searching “kidneys and hearts” and giving “to each of you according to your works.”
The Psalm names God as the One “who tests hearts and kidneys,” the title Christ claims as “the One who searcheth kidneys and hearts.”
The Son of Man “will repay each person according to his conduct,” matching “I will give to each of you according to your works.”

The Jerusalem letter says “to place no further burden upon you,” close to “I place no other burden upon you.” Acts attributes the decision to the Holy Spirit and the apostles, while Revelation gives it as Christ’s word.
Paul speaks of “the depths of God” revealed through the Spirit, a counterpart to “the deep things of Satan” claimed by the false teachers.
Both pair the command to “hold fast what thou hast” (Thyatira: “what ye have”) with Christ’s coming: “I am coming quickly” and “until I come.”

The Psalm’s promise, “I will give you nations as your inheritance,” lies behind “I will give authority over the nations.” In the Psalm the promise is to the anointed son; Revelation extends it to the conqueror.
Daniel says “authority” and rule over kingdoms are given “to a holy people of the Most High,” comparable to authority over the nations given to the faithful conqueror.
The promise to Laodicea likewise gives the conqueror a share in Christ’s rule, “to sit with Me on My throne.”

Revelation quotes Psalm 2:9: “You will shepherd them with an iron rod; you will crush them like a potter’s vessel.” Revelation applies to the conqueror the promise made in the Psalm to the anointed son.
The male child born to the woman is “to shepherd all the nations with an iron rod,” the same Psalm phrase applied directly to the Messiah.
The rider of Revelation 19 “will shepherd them with an iron rod,” the same phrase used here of the conqueror’s rule.
Jesus calls Himself “the bright morning star,” which identifies the gift of “the morning star” promised to the conqueror.
Peter speaks of “the morning star” rising “in your hearts,” the same image of the morning star given to believers.
Both use the identical refrain, “Let the one who hath an ear hear what the Spirit saith to the Churches.”
Paul says that the self-indulgent woman “is dead while living,” paralleling the Church that has “a name that thou livest, and thou art dead.”
The greeting of the book mentions “the seven spirits before His throne,” which Christ is said to have in the title of the letter to Sardis.
In the opening vision “He held seven stars in His right hand,” the “seven stars” named in Christ’s title for Sardis.

Both call for watchfulness in view of Christ’s sudden coming: “Blessed is the one who watcheth,” and “I am coming like a thief.” Revelation 16:15 adds keeping one’s garments, which the Sardis warning does not mention.
Jesus’ repeated command to “keep watch,” lest the master come and find them sleeping, parallels “Become watchful” addressed to a Church whose works were not found complete.

Both sayings have the Lord announcing that he will come “like a thief” and link this with watching. Revelation 16:15 adds a blessing on the one who keeps his garments, whereas the Sardis warning is addressed to a church that does not watch.
Both pair a call to watch with ignorance of the time of the coming: Sardis “shalt certainly not know at what hour,” and Matthew’s hearers “know neither the day nor the hour.”
Both use the image of coming “like a thief.” Paul applies it to “the day of the Lord,” while Revelation 3:3 has the speaker say “I will come like a thief” as a conditional warning.
The next verse continues the promise: those who “walk with Me in white” correspond to the conqueror who will be “clothed in white garments.”

Both speak of “white garments” given by the Lord to cover a person. Laodicea is counselled to buy them to hide its nakedness, whereas the few in Sardis are already said not to have defiled their garments.
Both use soiled clothing as an image of moral defilement: Sardis’ faithful “did not defile their garments,” and Jude speaks of “the tunic stained by the flesh.”

Both speak of names being erased from a book of life: the Psalm asks that the wicked “be erased from the book of the living,” while Revelation promises the conqueror, “I will certainly not erase his name from the book of life.”
Both promise that Jesus will acknowledge or confess the faithful person “before My Father.” Matthew conditions this on acknowledging Jesus before people; Revelation on conquering.
Both promise acknowledgement before the angels: Luke says the Son of Man will acknowledge “before the angels of God,” and Revelation “before His angels.”
Both verses contain the identical refrain “Let the one who hath an ear hear what the Spirit saith to the Churches.” In Revelation 2:7 it is followed by a promise to the conqueror.

The speaker to Philadelphia is “the Holy One, the True One,” and the martyrs address God as “Master, holy and true.” Revelation 6:10 uses the pair as an address in prayer rather than as a self-description.
Both describe Christ as holding a key or keys: “the key of David” here, and “the keys of death and Hades” in the inaugural vision.

Both describe authority connected with David that cannot be opposed: Isaiah’s figure receives “David’s glory” and rules “with no one contradicting,” and Christ opens and “no one will shut.” The Saints (Greek) wording of Isaiah has “David’s glory” rather than a key and does not mention opening and shutting.
The “opened door, which no one can shut” applies the title of the previous verse, the One who “openeth and no one will shut.”
Both churches are commended for not denying under pressure: Philadelphia “didst not deny My name,” and Pergamum “holdest fast My name and didst not deny My faith.”
Both commend those who have kept the word: Philadelphia “didst keep My word,” and Jesus says of his disciples, “they have kept Thy word,” in the context of revealing God’s name.
Both letters describe the same group in nearly the same words: “those who say that they themselves are Jews and are not” and “a synagogue of Satan.”

Both describe outsiders who will “bow” at the feet of God’s people, followed by recognition: Isaiah’s “You will know that I am the Lord” and Revelation’s “know that I loved thee.” In Isaiah it is kings and ruling women who bow to Zion.
Both have God declaring his love for his people with “I loved”: Isaiah “I loved you,” and Revelation, that opponents will “know that I loved thee.”

Both speak of the Lord keeping or rescuing the faithful from trial: Peter says the Lord knows how “to rescue the godly from trial,” and Revelation promises, “I also will keep thee from the hour of trial.”
Both join endurance with keeping: Philadelphia “didst keep the word of My endurance,” and Revelation 14:12 names “the endurance of the saints, those keeping the commandments of God.”

Both letters speak of a coming testing that is “about to” happen, Smyrna being told that the devil is about to imprison some “that ye may be tested.” Smyrna is told to endure the testing, whereas Philadelphia is promised to be kept from the hour of trial.
Both exhortations are nearly identical in substance: “Hold fast what thou hast” here, and to Thyatira, “Only hold fast what ye have until I come.”
Both contain the words “I am coming quickly.” Revelation 22:12 adds that the reward is with him, while here the concern is that no one take the believer’s crown.
Both speak of a crown held out to the faithful: Smyrna is promised “the crown of life” for faithfulness until death, and Philadelphia is warned that no one may take “thy crown.”
Both describe “new Jerusalem” coming down out of heaven from God; Revelation 21:2 shows in vision the city whose name is promised here.
Both describe the faithful bearing a divine name written on them: here “the name of My God,” and in Revelation 14:1 the Lamb’s name and “His Father’s name written upon their foreheads.”

Both promises to the one who conquers involve “a new name” written. In Revelation 2:17 the new name is written on a white stone and known only to the receiver, whereas here it is called “My new name.”
Both verses contain the identical refrain “Let the one who hath an ear hear what the Spirit saith to the Churches.” In Revelation 2:7 it is followed by a promise to the conqueror.
Both call Jesus Christ “the faithful witness”; Laodicea’s letter expands the title to “the faithful and true witness.”
Both apply the words “faithful” and “true” to Christ: here as “the faithful and true witness,” and in Revelation 19:11 the rider on the white horse “is called Faithful and True.”
Both connect the word “Amen” with Christ: he is called “the Amen” here, and Paul says that through him “is the ‘Amen’ to God.”
Both letters open their verdict with “I know thy works, that thou…” and then expose a hidden condition: Sardis “thou art dead,” Laodicea “neither cold nor hot.”
3:15 states the charge, “thou art neither cold nor hot,” and 3:16 draws the consequence for the one who is “lukewarm, and neither hot nor cold”: being vomited out of the Lord’s mouth.

Both quote a self-satisfied claim to wealth: Ephraim says, “Indeed I have become rich,” and Laodicea says, “I am rich and have become wealthy.” Hosea adds that his labours will not be found because of his injustices.
Both expose a church’s complacency with the words “become rich”: Paul ironically says, “Already you have become rich!” to the Corinthians, and Laodicea says, “I… have become wealthy.”
Both expose people who think they see while being blind: the Pharisees say “We see,” and Laodicea “knowest not that thou art… blind.”
The counsel answers the preceding diagnosis point by point: gold for the one who is “poor,” white garments for the “naked,” and eye salve for the “blind.”

Both link garments with avoiding the shame of nakedness: Laodicea is to clothe itself so that “the shame of thy nakedness may not be manifested,” and Revelation 16:15 blesses the one who keeps his garments “so that he may not walk naked and they see his shame.”
Both use gold tested or “refined by fire” as an image of value. Peter compares tested faith to such gold, whereas Revelation offers the gold itself as a purchase from the Lord.
Both state that discipline comes from love: “As many as I love, I reprove and discipline,” and “the Lord disciplines the one He loves.” Proverbs also speaks of being “corrected by Him.”
Both present the Lord’s reproof as something to accept: Job calls happy “the person whom the Lord reproved,” and Christ reproves those he loves.
Both describe the Lord’s discipline as an expression of a close relationship: Deuteronomy compares it to how “a man chastens his son,” while Revelation grounds it in love.
Both picture someone who “knocks” and those inside who should “open” to him, followed by a shared meal: Luke’s master has his slaves “recline at table,” and Christ will “dine with him.”

Both describe a beloved voice and knocking at a door with an appeal to open: “he knocks upon the door! Open to me.” In the Song the speaker hesitates to open; Revelation leaves the response to “anyone.”
Both promise that the Lord will come to the one who responds and remain with him: “I will come in unto him” and “We will come to him and make Our dwelling with him.”

Both promise that the faithful will sit on thrones alongside the Son: Matthew’s followers will “sit upon twelve thrones” when the Son of Man sits on “the throne of His glory.” Matthew specifies judging the twelve tribes; Revelation speaks of sharing Christ’s throne.
Revelation 20:4 shows faithful witnesses seated on “thrones” who “reigned with Christ,” corresponding to the promise that the conqueror will sit with Christ on his throne.
Both ground the believer’s hope in Christ’s own victory: “as I also conquered” and “I have overcome the world.” The English wording differs (“conquered” / “overcome”).
Both verses contain the identical refrain “Let the one who hath an ear hear what the Spirit saith to the Churches,” which closes each of the seven letters.
Both verses contain the identical refrain “Let the one who hath an ear hear what the Spirit saith to the Churches,” here closing the letters to Sardis and Laodicea.
Both verses contain the identical refrain “Let the one who hath an ear hear what the Spirit saith to the Churches,” here closing the letters to Philadelphia and Laodicea.
“The first voice I heard like a trumpet” refers back to the “loud voice like a trumpet” John heard in Revelation 1:10.
Both speak of things to take place “after these”: John was commanded to write them, and he is now invited up to be shown them.
Both contain a heavenly summons to ascend, “Come up hither” and “Come up here.” In Revelation 11:12 the two witnesses actually go up into heaven in a cloud.
Both prophets see the Lord “seated on a throne.” Isaiah locates the vision in the year of King Oziah’s death and describes the house full of his glory.
Both describe a vision of the Lord “sitting on His throne” with heavenly attendants around him. Micaiah’s vision is reported in a prophetic confrontation with the king.
Both open a vision with “I came to be in the Spirit.” In Revelation 1:10 this leads to hearing a trumpet-like voice; here to seeing the heavenly throne.

Both surround the divine throne with a bow-like radiance: Ezekiel sees “the appearance of a bow when it is in the cloud” all around, and John “a rainbow around the throne.” Ezekiel does not compare it to an emerald.
Both describe divine radiance as like “a jasper stone”: the One on the throne here, and the city “having the glory of God” in Revelation 21:11.
The jasper, sardius and emerald named here all appear among the foundation stones of the new Jerusalem, where they adorn the city rather than describe God’s appearance.
Both mention “the twenty-four elders” sitting upon thrones before God; Revelation 11:16 shows them falling to worship.
The “golden crowns” of the elders introduced here are the crowns they “throw… before the throne” in worship in Revelation 4:10.
The elders are “clothed in white garments,” the same clothing promised to the faithful conqueror in Revelation 3:5 (“clothed in white garments”).
Both describe God’s presence accompanied by thunder and lightning: at Sinai “thunder and lightning and a dark cloud,” and from the throne “lightnings and voices and thunders.”
Both visions feature “seven lamps.” Zechariah’s lamps are on a golden lampstand, whereas John’s are lamps of fire burning before the throne and are identified as the seven spirits of God.
Both locate “the seven spirits” before God’s throne, the same figure named in John’s opening greeting.
Both describe “something like a glassy sea” before God. In Revelation 15:2 it is “mixed with fire” and the conquerors stand upon it.
Both describe heavenly beings “full of eyes” all around. In Ezekiel the eyes cover the cherubim’s backs, hands, wings and wheels; John’s living creatures have no wheels.
Both describe four living beings associated with a lion, a calf, a human being and an eagle. In Ezekiel each creature has all four faces, whereas in Revelation each creature resembles one.
Both name God as “Lord God” and “Almighty” and as “the One who is and who was and who is coming,” though the order of the tenses differs.
Both address God as “Lord God Almighty, the One who… was and who is.” Revelation 11:17 omits “who is coming,” as God has now taken his power and reigned.
Both call God “the One living for the ages of the ages”; in Revelation 10:6 an angel swears by him as Creator.
Both describe God as the one who lives for ever: Daniel’s angelic figure swears “by God who lives for ever,” and the living creatures honour “the One living for the ages of the ages.”

Both describe heavenly beings giving honour and glory “to the One sitting upon the throne” for “the ages of the ages.” In Revelation 5:13 the praise is shared with the Lamb and is answered by the living creatures’ “Amen.”
Both show “the twenty-four elders” falling before God and worshipping; in Revelation 11:16 they are described as sitting upon their thrones before God.
Both show the twenty-four elders falling and worshipping God who sits upon the throne, and both introduce their spoken response.
The crowns the elders throw before the throne are the “golden crowns” on their heads described in Revelation 4:4.
Both acclaim one who is “worthy… to receive” power, honour and glory. Here God is praised as Creator; in Revelation 5:12 the Lamb is praised as the one who was slaughtered.
Both ground worship in God’s creating work: here “Thou didst create all things,” and the angel calls all to “worship the One who made heaven and the earth and sea.”
Both describe God as the creator of all: the angel swears by the One “who created heaven and the things in it, and the earth… and the sea.”

Both describe a scroll held in a heavenly hand with writing on both sides: Ezekiel’s scroll had “writing on the back and the front,” John’s is “written within and on the back.” Ezekiel’s scroll is unrolled, whereas John’s is sealed.
Both describe a sealed book that cannot be read: Isaiah’s “sealed book,” and the scroll “sealed with seven seals.”
The scroll seen in the right hand of the One sitting upon the throne is taken from that hand by the Lamb in Revelation 5:7.
The angel’s question about who is worthy to open the scroll and its seals is answered in Revelation 5:5: the Lion of Judah “conquered, to open the scroll and its seven seals.”
Both describe a sealed book that no one can read: in Isaiah one says, “I cannot read, for it is sealed.” Isaiah addresses spiritual blindness; Revelation asks who is worthy to open the scroll.
Revelation 10:1 introduces “another mighty angel,” recalling the mighty angel proclaiming here.

Both use the three-part range “in heaven… upon the earth… beneath the earth.” Here no one in those realms can open the scroll; in Revelation 5:13 every creature in them praises the One on the throne and the Lamb.

Both describe revealed matters that remain closed to the seer: Daniel’s words are “covered and sealed,” and no one is found worthy to open John’s scroll. Daniel is told to go away, whereas John weeps.
Both use the title “Root… of David” for Jesus; in Revelation 22:16 Jesus calls himself “the Root and the offspring of David.”
Both use the image of a root from David’s line: Isaiah speaks of “Jesse’s root” and one rising to rule nations, and Revelation of “the Root of David.”
Both identify Christ as coming from the tribe of Judah: Hebrews says our Lord “has sprung from Judah,” and Revelation calls him “the Lion from the tribe of Judah.”
Both speak of seven eyes ranging over all the earth: Zechariah’s “seven are the Lord’s eyes, looking over all the earth,” and the Lamb’s “seven eyes… sent into all the earth.”
Both present an object with “seven eyes.” In Zechariah the eyes are on a stone set before Joshua; here they belong to the Lamb.
Both describe Christ as “the Lamb slaughtered,” a title Revelation 13:8 connects with the book of life.
The Lamb takes the scroll “from the right hand of the One sitting upon the throne,” where John first saw it in Revelation 5:1.
Both liken prayer to incense: the Psalmist asks that his “prayer be directed as incense,” and the golden bowls of incense “are the prayers of the saints.”
Both connect incense with “the prayers of the saints” offered before God’s throne. In Revelation 8:3–4 an angel offers it at the golden altar with a golden censer.
Both speak of singing “a new song” to God. In the Psalm it is put into the singer’s mouth after deliverance; here it is sung to the Lamb who was slaughtered.

relationship: shared theme of purchase by blood
rationale: Both speak of a people acquired by blood: the Lamb “didst purchase for God in Thy blood” people, and God’s Church was “acquired through His own blood.”
Both use the fourfold list of nation, tribe, tongue and people to describe the whole human range. In Revelation 14:6 they are recipients of the good news; here they are those purchased.
Both state that Christ made his people “a kingdom” and “priests” to God, the second passage adding that “they shall reign upon the earth.”
Both describe God’s people as royal and priestly: Israel is to be “a royal priesthood and a holy nation,” and the redeemed are made “a kingdom and priests unto our God.”
Both say the redeemed will be “priests” of God and will “reign.” Revelation 20:6 specifies a reign with Christ for a thousand years.
Both count the heavenly attendants in the same paired form: Daniel’s “a thousand thousands… ten thousand times ten thousand,” and John’s “myriads of myriads and thousands of thousands.”
Both describe the angels gathered around the throne together with the elders and the four living creatures.
Both speak of “myriads of angels” in God’s heavenly presence; Hebrews places them in festive gathering at the heavenly Jerusalem.
Both acclaim one who is worthy “to receive” power, honour and glory. Revelation 4:11 addresses God as Creator; here the Lamb is praised as slaughtered.
Both list seven attributes of praise, sharing power, wisdom, strength, honour, glory and blessing. Revelation 7:12 has “thanksgiving” where this verse has “wealth,” and ascribes them to God.
Both declare the Lamb “worthy” because he was “slaughtered”; the new song of Revelation 5:9 is taken up here by the angels.
Both describe universal homage from those “in heaven and on earth and under the earth.” Philippians speaks of bending the knee at the name of Jesus; Revelation adds the sea.
Both ascribe praise jointly “to the One sitting upon the throne” and “to the Lamb”; in Revelation 7:10 the praise is for salvation.
Both doxologies ascribe “the glory and the dominion for the ages of the ages.” In Revelation 1:6 they are ascribed to Christ alone.
Both show the four living creatures and the elders responding with “Amen” as the elders fall and worship; Revelation 19:4 adds “Hallelujah.”
Both describe the living creatures giving praise and the elders falling to worship before the throne, the pattern established in Revelation 4:9–11.
The Lamb now begins to open the “seven seals” of the scroll first seen in Revelation 5:1.
The Lamb who was declared able to “open the scroll and its seven seals” and took the scroll in Revelation 5:5–7 now opens the first seal.
Both describe a seal being opened followed by a living creature saying, “Come.” Revelation 6:3 continues the sequence with the second seal.
Both visions include “white horses” that go out across the earth among horses of other colours. In Zechariah the horses draw chariots and are identified as the four winds of heaven.
Both visions include a mounted rider and a white horse. In Zechariah the white horses are among several colours behind a man on a flame-red horse.

Both open with “behold, a white horse” and a rider associated with crowns and warfare. The texts do not by themselves establish that the two riders are the same; the rider of Revelation 19 is called Faithful and True.
Both describe a seal being opened followed by a living creature saying, “Come,” this verse continuing the sequence begun at the first seal.
“The second living creature” speaking here is the one described in Revelation 4:7 as “like a calf.”
Both visions include red horses among horses of several colours sent out by God: Zechariah’s first chariot “had flame-red horses,” and John sees a horse “fiery red.”
Both visions feature a rider on a red horse: Zechariah sees “a man mounted on a flame-red horse.” Zechariah’s rider is not given a sword or the power to take peace.

Both pair the removal of peace on the earth with a sword: Jesus did not come “to bring peace upon the earth… but a sword,” and the rider is given “to take peace from the earth” and “a great sword.” Jesus speaks of division his coming brings, not of mutual slaughter.
Both use the weighing of food as a sign of scarcity: Jerusalem will “eat bread by weight and in need,” and the rider holds “a balance in his hand.”
Both use rationing by weight as a sign of judgement: God threatens that bread will be given back “by weight” and they will not be filled. Revelation shows the balance without stating the threat.
Both visions include “black horses” among horses of several colours; in Zechariah they draw the second chariot.

Both contain a command limiting the scope of a judgement by telling agents “not to harm” certain produce or vegetation: here “the oil and the wine,” in Revelation 9:4 “the grass of the earth or any green thing or any tree.” In Revelation 9:4 people without God’s seal are then targeted.

Both verses use the same pattern for the seal openings: when He opened a numbered seal, the matching numbered living creature is heard saying “Come.” Revelation 6:3 gives the second instance and 6:7 the fourth.
Revelation 4:7 introduces the “fourth living creature” who speaks at the fourth seal, describing it as “like an eagle flying.” The seal vision itself does not repeat this description.

Ezekiel divides the judgment by quarters, with portions consumed “by death,” “by famine” and falling “by the sword.” Revelation gives authority over “a fourth of the earth” to kill with sword, famine and death; Ezekiel's fourth portion is scattering rather than beasts.

Ezekiel 5:17 names famine, “harmful wild animals,” death and the sword as judgments sent by the Lord. Revelation's rider kills “with sword and with famine and with death and by the beasts of the earth,” the same four agents.

Both passages treat Death and Hades as a personified pair: here Death rides and “Hades followed with him,” while in Revelation 20:13–14 “Death and Hades” give up their dead and are thrown into the lake of fire.

Both visions show “the souls” of those killed “because of the word of God” and because of testimony. Revelation 20:4 specifies they were beheaded for “the testimony of Jesus” and adds that they reign with Christ, whereas 6:9 places them “beneath the altar.”
John is on Patmos “because of the word of God and the testimony of Jesus,” the same twofold cause given for the slaughter of the souls under the altar. John's case involves exile rather than death.

The martyrs ask when God will “judge and avenge our blood”; Revelation 19:2 declares that He “judged the great prostitute” and “avenged the blood of His slaves.” Both also describe God's judging as “true.”

The psalm asks that “vengeance for the poured-out blood of Thy servants be known among the nations.” The martyrs' cry likewise seeks vengeance for their blood, though it is addressed directly to the “Master, holy and true.”

Both open an appeal to God in heaven with the question “how long,” addressed to a sovereign title (“Lord Almighty”; “O Master”). Zechariah's angel asks about mercy for Jerusalem, whereas the martyrs ask for judgment and vengeance.

The white robe given to each martyr reappears in the great multitude “clothed in white robes” before the throne in Revelation 7:9. The later vision does not state that this multitude consists only of martyrs.

Daniel is told to “go and rest,” for there are still days “until completion is fulfilled.” The martyrs are likewise told to rest “for a little time yet” until the number of their fellow slaves is complete.

Revelation 14:13 says the dead who die in the Lord “rest from their labours.” This connects with the instruction that the slain souls should “rest for a little time,” though 14:13 does not mention a waiting period.

Isaiah says God will “clothe heaven in darkness and make its covering like sackcloth.” Revelation describes the sun becoming “black like a haircloth sack.” Isaiah speaks of heaven generally, not the sun in particular.

Joel describes the earth in turmoil, heaven shaken, and “the sun and moon will grow dark.” The sixth seal joins an earthquake with a darkened sun and altered moon, though Joel does not say the moon becomes like blood.

Jesus foretells that “the sun will be darkened, the moon will not give its brightness” and the heavens shaken. The sixth seal shows the same failure of sun and moon, adding the great earthquake and blood-like moon.

Isaiah 34:4 pictures the stars falling “like leaves falling from a fig tree.” Revelation likewise compares falling stars to a fig tree shedding its figs; Isaiah speaks of leaves, Revelation of unripe figs shaken by wind.
Jesus foretells that “the stars will fall from heaven,” the same event shown here as “the stars of heaven fell to the earth.” Matthew does not use the fig-tree comparison.
Isaiah says “heaven will roll up like a scroll,” and Revelation says heaven withdrew “like a scroll being rolled up.” The image and comparison are the same in both texts.

At the seventh bowl “every island fled, and mountains were not found,” echoing the sixth seal's “every mountain and island were moved from their places.” The bowl text speaks of disappearance rather than displacement.

Before the great white throne “the earth and heaven fled, and no place was found for them,” comparable to heaven withdrawing and mountains and islands moved from their places. Revelation 20:11 is set at the final judgment.

Isaiah describes people going “into caves, into clefts in the rocks” from the Lord's terror when He rises to shatter the earth. Revelation shows the kings and all classes hiding “in the caves and among the rocks of the mountains.”

Isaiah 2:10 commands “enter the rocks and hide in the earth from the Lord's terror.” Revelation describes people of every rank who “hid themselves” among the rocks; Isaiah's verse is an imperative, Revelation's a narrative.

Hosea has the people say to the mountains “Cover us!” and to the hills “Fall upon us!” Revelation repeats the cry “Fall upon us and hide us” addressed to the mountains and rocks, adding hiding from the face of the One on the throne and the Lamb's wrath.
Jesus says people will begin “to say to the mountains, ‘Fall upon us,’ and to the hills, ‘Cover us.’” Revelation uses the same cry to the mountains, “Fall upon us.”

The people seek to hide “from the face of the One sitting upon the throne,” and Revelation 20:11 describes the One sitting on the throne “from whose face the earth and heaven fled.” Both stress flight from His face.
Malachi asks “who will stand at his appearance?” concerning the day of the Lord's coming. Revelation closes with the same question, “who is able to stand?” on the great day of wrath.
Joel declares that “the Lord's day is great” and asks “who will be sufficient for it?” Revelation likewise speaks of “the great day” and asks who is able to stand.

Zephaniah calls the Lord's “great day” a “day of wrath,” the combination used in “the great day of Their wrath.” Zephaniah's day falls on the earth's inhabitants; Revelation attributes the wrath to the One on the throne and the Lamb.
The restraint of the winds so that none might blow “upon the earth or upon the sea or upon any tree” is explained in 7:3: “Do not harm the earth or the sea or the trees” until the sealing is done.

Daniel sees “four winds of heaven falling upon the great sea,” and Revelation sees four angels holding “the four winds of the earth” back from the earth and sea. In Daniel the winds are released; here they are restrained.

Jesus says His angels will gather the chosen “from the four winds,” and Revelation pairs angels with the four winds in connection with God's slaves. In Matthew the angels gather; here they restrain the winds until the sealing.
The angel carrying “a seal of the living God” commands in 7:3 that harm wait until “we seal the slaves of our God upon their foreheads,” and 7:4–8 then numbers those sealed.
The locusts of Revelation 9:4 may harm only those “who do not have the seal of God upon their foreheads,” showing the protective purpose of the seal brought by this angel.

In Ezekiel a man is sent to “put the sign upon the foreheads” of the faithful before judgment falls, as the angels here seal God's slaves “upon their foreheads” before harm is done. Ezekiel speaks of a sign, Revelation of a seal.
Revelation 9:4 restricts the locusts from harming grass or trees and directs them only at those without “the seal of God upon their foreheads,” the seal applied in 7:3.
The hundred forty-four thousand reappear with the Lamb on Mount Zion, having His name and His Father's name “written upon their foreheads,” which corresponds to the sealing on the forehead here.

Revelation 14:1 shows the Lamb on Mount Zion with “a hundred forty-four thousand” bearing names on their foreheads, the same number as those sealed here. Chapter 14 does not repeat the tribal arrangement.
Revelation 14:3 again names “the hundred forty-four thousand,” described as “purchased from the earth,” who alone can learn the new song. It shares the number but does not mention Israel's tribes.
Exodus lists the sons of Israel, including Reuben, Judah and Gad, the three tribes named in this verse. Revelation's order differs, placing Judah first.
Asher, Naphtali and Manasseh, each with “twelve thousand,” belong to the list whose total is announced in 7:4: “a hundred forty-four thousand, sealed from every tribe of the sons of Israel.”

Genesis lists the sons of Leah as including Simeon, Levi and Issachar, the three tribes named consecutively in this verse. Genesis also names Reuben, Judah and Zebulun, who appear elsewhere in Revelation's list.
The last three tribes, each with “twelve thousand sealed,” close the list whose total is announced in 7:4: “a hundred forty-four thousand, sealed from every tribe of the sons of Israel.”

Revelation 5:9 says the Lamb purchased people “from every tribe and tongue and people and nation”; the great multitude is drawn “from every nation and tribes and peoples and tongues.” The fourfold formula is shared, in different order.

The martyrs under the altar are each given “a white robe,” and the great multitude stands “clothed in white robes.” Revelation 6:11 concerns a limited group awaiting completion; 7:9 a multitude no one could number.
In John 12:13 the crowd takes “branches of the palm trees” to greet the King of Israel. The multitude likewise holds “palm branches” before the throne and the Lamb.
The psalm declares “Salvation belongs to the Lord,” and the multitude cries “Salvation belongeth to our God.” Revelation adds the One sitting upon the throne and the Lamb as joint recipients.

A great multitude in heaven proclaims “The salvation and the glory and the power belong to our God,” with a loud voice, as the multitude does here. Revelation 19:1 adds glory and power and the call “Hallelujah.”
Both acclamations are addressed jointly “to the One sitting upon the throne and to the Lamb.” Revelation 5:13 ascribes blessing, honour, glory and dominion rather than salvation.

Revelation 5:11 shows “many angels around the throne and the living creatures and the elders,” the same arrangement given here. In chapter 5 the angels sing; here they fall on their faces and worship.
The elders “fell upon their faces and worshipped God,” the identical action here ascribed to all the angels. Revelation 11:16 concerns the twenty-four elders only.

Revelation 5:12 ascribes power, wisdom, strength, honour, glory and blessing to the Lamb, and 5:13–14 ends with “for the ages of the ages” and “Amen.” Chapter 7's sevenfold list replaces wealth with thanksgiving and is addressed to “our God.”

Jude closes by ascribing glory, majesty, might and authority to God “into all the ages. Amen.” The shared elements are the ascription of attributes to God, the reference to the ages and the closing Amen; the lists of attributes differ largely.
The elder's question concerns “these who are clothed in the white robes,” the great multitude seen in 7:9 “clothed in white robes” before the throne.
In both scenes “one of the elders” speaks to John to explain what he sees. In 5:5 the elder comforts and announces the Lion of Judah; here he asks a question to prompt the explanation.

Revelation 22:14 blesses “they who wash their robes,” echoing those who “washed their robes and made them white.” Chapter 22 links the washing to access to the tree of life rather than to the great tribulation.
The faithful conquer “because of the blood of the Lamb,” as here their robes are made white “in the blood of the Lamb.” Revelation 12:11 adds the word of their testimony.

Isaiah promises that sins like scarlet will be whitened “like snow” and “like wool.” Revelation likewise speaks of robes made white, though by the blood of the Lamb rather than by direct divine pardon as in Isaiah.

The promise that the One on the throne “will spread His tent over them” corresponds to the announcement “the tabernacle of God is with men, and He shall dwell with them.” Revelation 21:3 is set in the new Jerusalem.
In the new city “the throne of God and of the Lamb” is present and “His slaves will serve Him,” echoing those before the throne who “serve Him day and night.”

Isaiah promises a covering over Mount Zion by day and night, “shelter and concealment” from heat and rain. Revelation pictures God spreading His tent over the redeemed; Isaiah speaks of cloud and shade rather than a tent.

Isaiah says “they will neither hunger nor thirst, nor will scorching heat or the sun strike them,” which Revelation reproduces nearly word for word. Isaiah's next words about leading them to springs of water are echoed in Revelation 7:17.
The psalm promises that “the sun will not scorch you,” the same protection from the sun given to those before the throne. The psalm also includes the moon by night.
Isaiah says God “removed every tear from every face,” the image behind “God will wipe every tear from their eyes.” Isaiah connects it with death being swallowed.
Revelation 21:4 repeats “He shall wipe away every tear from their eyes” in the new creation, adding that death, mourning, crying and pain will be no more.
God promises to the thirsty “the spring of the water of life,” matching the Lamb's guiding them to “springs of waters of life.” In 21:6 the speaker is the Alpha and the Omega on the throne.
The seventh seal is the last of the “seven seals” on the scroll held by the One on the throne in Revelation 5:1; its opening completes that series.
Revelation 6:12 opens the sixth seal with the same formula, “when He opened the … seal.” The sixth seal brings earthquake and cosmic upheaval, whereas the seventh brings silence.
Gabriel identifies himself as one “who stands before God,” the description given to the seven angels here. Luke names one angel; Revelation speaks of seven unnamed angels.
Revelation 11:15 records the sounding of the seventh angel, completing the series of trumpets given to the seven angels in 8:2.

Revelation 5:8 describes “golden bowls full of incense, which are the prayers of the saints,” and here incense is offered “with the prayers of all the saints.” In 5:8 the elders and living creatures hold the bowls; here an angel with a golden censer offers the incense.
The psalmist asks, “Let my prayer be directed as incense before Thee.” Revelation pictures incense offered with the saints' prayers before the throne.
Revelation 9:13 mentions a voice from the horns of “the golden altar before God,” the same altar on which the incense is offered here.
The psalm asks that prayer be directed “as incense before Thee,” and Revelation shows the smoke of incense rising “with the prayers of the saints … before God.”
Revelation 8:3 describes the angel with the golden censer receiving incense to offer with the saints' prayers; 8:4 describes the smoke of that incense going up before God.

In Ezekiel the man in the robe is told to “fill your hands with burning coals” and “scatter them over the city.” The angel likewise fills the censer from the fire of the altar and throws it to the earth; Ezekiel's coals come from among the cherubim.

Leviticus prescribes a “firepan full of burning coals from the altar,” the equipment and source of fire used by the angel here. In Leviticus the coals are taken within the veil with incense, not thrown out in judgment.
Revelation 11:19 lists “lightnings and voices and thunders and an earthquake” when God's temple is opened, the same phenomena as here. Revelation 11:19 adds great hail.
Revelation 8:2 introduces the seven angels before God to whom “seven trumpets were given”; 8:6 shows the same angels preparing to sound them.
The psalm recalls that God made Egypt's rains “hail, consuming fire in their land.” The first trumpet likewise brings hail and fire on the earth, adding blood and the burning of a third.
Ezekiel's judgment on Gog includes “blood,” “hailstones” and raining fire, the three elements of the first trumpet. Ezekiel adds death, flooding rain and sulfur.
Joel foretells wonders in heaven and on earth: “blood, fire and a vapor of smoke.” The first trumpet combines fire and blood thrown to the earth, but Joel does not mention hail.

God threatens to make the destroying mountain “like a burned mountain” and roll it down. Revelation sees “something like a great mountain burning with fire” thrown into the sea; Jeremiah's oracle concerns a named enemy power, not the sea.
In Exodus the river's water “turned to blood” and its fish died. The second trumpet turns a third of the sea into blood, extending the plague from river to sea and limiting it to a third.
At the second bowl the sea becomes blood and “every living soul died, the things in the sea.” The second trumpet affects only a third of the sea creatures and also destroys ships.
In Exodus “the fish in the river died” when the water became blood. The trumpet likewise brings death to living creatures in waters turned to blood, though in the sea and limited to a third.

The third bowl is poured “into the rivers and the springs of the waters,” the same targets struck by the falling star at the third trumpet. The bowl turns them into blood; the trumpet affects a third of them.
At the fifth trumpet John sees “a star fallen from heaven to the earth,” another falling star in the same trumpet series. The fifth-trumpet star receives the key of the abyss.

Isaiah laments that the “dawn-bearer” fell “from heaven” and was shattered to earth. Revelation sees a great star falling from heaven; Isaiah's taunt is directed at a ruler and does not mention waters.

God threatens to “give them bitter water to drink” as judgment. Revelation describes waters made bitter so that many died; Jeremiah's judgment is on Jerusalem's prophets and does not name wormwood in this rendering.

God says He will “make them drink gall-water” as punishment. Revelation's waters turned to wormwood and made bitter carry the same idea of judgment by poisoned water, though this rendering of Jeremiah says gall rather than wormwood.

Isaiah foretells that heaven's stars “will not give light,” the sun will grow dark and “the moon will not give its light.” The fourth trumpet strikes sun, moon and stars so that they are darkened, limited to a third.
Joel says “the sun and moon will grow dark, and the stars will sink their brightness,” the same three lights darkened at the fourth trumpet. Revelation limits the darkening to a third.

Jesus foretells that the sun will be darkened, the moon will not give its brightness and the stars will fall. The fourth trumpet darkens sun, moon and stars partially; Matthew has the stars fall rather than dim.
Revelation 9:12 announces “The one woe hath passed” with two woes still to come, counting off the threefold “Woe, woe, woe” proclaimed here for the remaining trumpets.
Revelation 11:14 announces that the second woe has passed and “the third woe is coming quickly,” continuing the series of three woes announced by the eagle.

An angel is seen “flying in midheaven” to address those on the earth, as the eagle flies “in midheaven” crying to “those dwelling upon the earth.” The angel brings eternal good news, the eagle a message of woe.
Revelation 20:1 shows an angel coming down from heaven “having the key of the abyss,” the same key given here to the fallen star. In chapter 20 the key is used to bind Satan.
Revelation 9:2 continues the scene: the one given the key “opened the shaft of the abyss,” releasing smoke that darkens the sun.
At the third trumpet “a great star fell from heaven,” as at the fifth trumpet John sees “a star fallen from heaven.” The third-trumpet star falls on waters; this one receives the key of the abyss.

Abraham sees a flame rising from the land of Sodom “as the vapour of a furnace.” Revelation describes smoke going up from the abyss “like smoke of a great furnace,” a similar comparison applied to a different source.
Joel describes the locust army's day with “the sun and moon will grow dark.” Here the smoke that releases the locusts darkens “the sun and the air”; Joel does not attribute the darkening to smoke.
Joel describes a devouring plague of locusts sent as judgment. Revelation's locusts come from the smoke of the abyss and are given authority like scorpions, unlike Joel's crop-devouring insects.
Revelation 9:10 explains the scorpion-like authority: the locusts “have tails like scorpions and stings,” and in their tails is their authority to harm people.
Revelation 7:3 commands that the earth, sea and trees not be harmed until God's slaves are sealed “upon their foreheads.” Here the locusts may harm only those who lack that seal.
In Ezekiel 9:4 a sign is put “upon the foreheads” of the faithful before judgment. Revelation's locusts harm only those without “the seal of God upon their foreheads.”

Ezekiel's executioners are told, “do not approach anyone upon whom the sign is.” The locusts are likewise restrained from those bearing God's seal; Ezekiel's judgment kills, whereas the locusts torment.
Revelation 9:10 restates the locusts' authority “to harm people for five months” and locates their sting in scorpion-like tails, matching the five months of scorpion-like torment here.
The Lord permits the devil to harm Job but says “only preserve his life.” The locusts are likewise permitted to torment but “not to kill.”

Job speaks of those “who long for death and do not obtain it,” digging for it as for treasure. Revelation describes people who “will seek death and will certainly not find it.” Job speaks of sufferers in general, not a period of judgment.
Joel's locust army has an “appearance … like the sight of horses” and is “arrayed for war.” Revelation's locusts are “like horses prepared for war”; Joel does not mention crowns or human faces.
Joel says of the invading locust nation, “Its teeth are a lion's teeth.” Revelation's locusts likewise have teeth “like lions' teeth”; Joel does not mention hair.

Joel's locusts move “with a sound like chariots” and are “arrayed for war.” Revelation compares the sound of the locusts' wings to “chariots of many horses running to war”; Joel does not mention breastplates.
The cavalry of the sixth trumpet also wear breastplates, described as “fiery red and hyacinth blue and sulfur yellow,” paralleling the locusts' breastplates “like iron breastplates.”
Both verses describe the locusts’ power to hurt people for “five months” and compare it to a scorpion. Revelation 9:5 adds that they are not allowed to kill, only to torment.
Revelation 9:3 introduces the locusts as given “authority” like that of “the scorpions of the earth”. Revelation 9:10 locates this authority in their scorpion-like tails.

Both verses say the creatures’ “authority” is “in their tails” and that with them they “harm”. Revelation 9:19 speaks of the horses of the sixth trumpet, whose tails are like snakes, not of the scorpion-like locusts.

Revelation 9:1–2 opens “the shaft of the abyss”, from which the locusts come. Revelation 9:11 names their king as “the angel of the abyss”. The earlier passage does not say whether the fallen star is the same figure as this angel.
Both verses use the same formula to mark the series of woes: “The one woe hath passed” and “The second woe hath passed”, each followed by “Behold” and an announcement of what is still to come.

The eagle’s triple “Woe, woe, woe” in Revelation 8:13 announces the three woes tied to the last trumpets. Revelation 9:12 marks the end of the first of these, which followed the fifth angel’s trumpet in 9:1–2.

Both passages name “the golden altar” before God. In Revelation 8:3–5 the saints’ prayers are offered on it and fire from it is thrown to the earth before the trumpets begin; in 9:13 a voice comes from its horns.

Exodus 30:2–3 prescribes an object with “horns of one piece with it”, all overlaid “with pure gold”. Revelation 9:13 speaks of “the horns of the golden altar”. The verses shown do not themselves name the object, which is introduced in the verse before them.
Revelation 9:15 carries out the command of 9:14: “the four angels” are “loosed” and are said to have been prepared for a set hour so that they might kill a third of the people.
Both the sixth trumpet and the sixth bowl are directed at “the great river Euphrates”. In 16:12 the river is dried up to prepare the way of kings from the east; in 9:14 four angels are bound there.
Revelation 9:18 reports the outcome of 9:15: “a third of the people were killed”, using the same wording as the purpose given for the release of the four angels.
Both verses give a number of “myriads of myriads”. In Revelation 5:11 they are angels around the throne; here they are mounted armies.

Daniel 7:10 counts “ten thousand times ten thousand” standing before the Ancient One, a figure close to Revelation’s “two myriads of myriads”. Daniel’s host attends a heavenly court, not a cavalry army.
In both verses the seer reports a number he did not see but heard: “I heard the number”. Revelation 7:4 gives the number of those sealed; 9:16 the number of the cavalry.
Revelation 9:18 repeats “fire and smoke and sulfur” coming out of the horses’ mouths and calls them three plagues that killed a third of the people.

Both the locusts of the fifth trumpet and the cavalry of the sixth are described as wearing “breastplates”. The locusts’ breastplates are “like iron breastplates”; the riders’ are fiery red, hyacinth blue and sulfur yellow.
Revelation 9:17 describes the “fire and smoke and sulfur” coming from the horses’ mouths, which 9:18 identifies as the three plagues.
Revelation 9:15 states the purpose of the four angels’ release, “so that they might kill a third of the people”. Revelation 9:18 reports that this happened.

Both verses place the creatures’ “authority” “in their tails” and say they “harm” with them. Revelation 9:10 concerns the scorpion-tailed locusts; 9:19 the horses whose tails are like snakes with heads.
Revelation 9:21 continues the same sentence of judgment: those who survived the plagues “did not repent” of their murders, sorceries, sexual immorality or thefts, as well as of their idolatry.
Jeremiah 1:16 condemns those who “bowed down to the works of their hands”. Revelation 9:20 uses the same phrase, “the works of their hands”, for the idols that the survivors kept worshipping.

Daniel 5:23 rebukes a king who “praised all the idols made by human hands” but did not bless the living God. The Daniel text shown does not list the idols’ materials or say they cannot see or hear, as Revelation 9:20 does.

Revelation 21:8 names “murderers”, the “sexually immoral” and “sorcerers” among those whose share is in the lake of fire. These are three of the four sins of which the survivors in 9:21 do not repent.
Revelation 22:15 places “the sorcerers and the sexually immoral and the murderers” outside the city. These match three of the four sins named in 9:21.
Matthew 15:19 lists “murders”, “sexual immoralities” and “thefts” among the evils that come out of the heart. Three of the four sins in Revelation 9:21 appear, but sorcery does not.
Revelation 10:1 introduces “another mighty angel”, which recalls the “mighty angel” of 5:2. Both angels are linked with a scroll.
Ezekiel compares the brightness around the Lord’s glory to “a bow when it is in the cloud”. Revelation’s angel is “clothed with a cloud” and has “the rainbow upon his head”.

Both descriptions give the figure a face or appearance “like the sun” and describe his feet: “like burnished bronze” in 1:15 and “like pillars of fire” in 10:1. In chapter 1 the figure is the risen Christ; in chapter 10 he is called an angel.
Revelation 10:8–10 returns to “the opened scroll” in the hand of the angel “standing upon the sea and upon the earth”. There the seer takes the little scroll and eats it.
Revelation 10:5 again describes the angel as “standing upon the sea and upon the earth”, the stance set up in 10:2.
In Ezekiel a hand holds out “a scroll of a book” and unrolls it before the prophet; Revelation’s angel holds “a little scroll opened”. Both scrolls are later given to the seer to eat.

Amos 3:8 sets a lion’s roar beside the Lord’s speaking, and Revelation 10:3 compares the angel’s loud cry to a lion that roars. In both, the roar comes before divine speech: prophecy in Amos, the seven thunders in Revelation.
Isaiah compares the Lord to a lion that “cries over prey”, filling the mountains with its voice. Revelation 10:3 likewise says the angel “cried with a loud voice just as a lion roareth”.
Daniel is told to “seal the book until the time of completion”, and the seer is told to “Seal up” what the seven thunders spoke. In Revelation the seer is also forbidden to write the words at all.

Revelation 22:10 reverses the command of 10:4: “Do not seal the words of the prophecy of this scroll, for the time is near.” The thunders’ words stay sealed, while the book of the prophecy itself is left open.
Daniel 12:9 says “the commands are covered and sealed” until a set time. This is another Danielic instance of sealing revelation, the action commanded in Revelation 10:4.
Both figures raise a hand “to heaven” and swear by the One who lives for ever about when the end will come. Daniel’s figure raises both right and left hands; Revelation’s angel raises his right hand.

In Deuteronomy the Lord says, “I will lift My hand unto heaven, and swear”, together with “I live for ever”. Revelation 10:5–6 combines the same raised hand with an oath by the One who lives for ever.
Revelation 10:2 sets the angel’s right foot on the sea and his left on the earth, the stance behind the phrase “standing upon the sea and upon the earth” in 10:5.
Both verses call God “the One living for the ages of the ages”. Revelation 4:9 uses it of the One sitting upon the throne; 10:6 uses it in the angel’s oath.
Revelation 4:11 praises God because He “didst create all things”. The oath in 10:6 identifies Him at length as the One who created heaven, earth and sea and the things in them.

Revelation 10:7 points to the days when the seventh angel is about to sound. In 11:15–18 “the seventh angel sounded”, God is said to have reigned, and the reward is given to “Thy slaves the prophets”.
Amos 3:7 says the Lord does nothing without revealing it “to His servants the prophets”. Revelation 10:7 says God announced His mystery “to His own slaves, the prophets”.
Revelation 10:2 first shows the angel with “a little scroll opened” in his hand, his feet upon the sea and the earth. In 10:8 the seer is told to take that scroll.
The “voice from heaven” that forbade writing in 10:4 speaks “again” in 10:8. Revelation 10:5 gives the description of the angel “standing upon the sea and upon the earth” that 10:8 repeats.

Ezekiel is told to “eat this scroll”, his belly is to be filled with it, and in his mouth it is “like sweet honey”. Revelation 10:9 takes up the scroll, the eating, the belly and sweetness “as honey” in the mouth, and adds that it will make the belly bitter.
Ezekiel 2:8 tells the prophet to “Open your mouth wide and eat what I give you”. This is the command that leads to his eating the scroll, which Revelation 10:9 echoes in “Take and devour it”.

Both prophets eat a scroll given to them, and in Ezekiel’s words it was “in my mouth” “like sweet honey”, as in Revelation’s “in my mouth it was sweet as honey”. Ezekiel 3:3 mentions the belly being filled but not made bitter.
The psalmist says God’s sayings are sweet “beyond honey” to “my mouth”. Revelation 10:10 gives the same sweetness in the mouth to the scroll the seer eats.

The scroll Ezekiel is given to eat has written on it “a lament, a song and woe”. This sorrowful content is set beside the sweetness in the mouth, much as Revelation sets the bitter belly beside the sweet taste. Ezekiel does not himself speak of bitterness here.

Jeremiah is given the Lord’s words in his mouth and appointed “over nations and kingdoms”. Revelation 10:11 commissions the seer to prophesy concerning “peoples and nations and tongues and many kings”.
Revelation 11:9 uses the same group of terms as 10:11, “the peoples and tribes and tongues and nations”, for those who look on the dead witnesses.
Revelation 14:6 sends a message to “every nation and tribe and tongue and people”. This is a proclamation to the same universal audience as in 10:11.

Ezekiel’s guide measures the house all around “with the measuring reed”, “to distinguish between the holy areas and the forewall”. Revelation 11:1 gives the seer a reed to measure the temple of God, and 11:2 excludes the outer court.
Revelation 21:15 has a “golden measuring reed” used to measure the city, its gates and its wall. In 11:1 the seer himself is given a reed to measure the temple, altar and worshippers.
Zechariah sees a man with “a land-measuring cord” going “To measure Jerusalem”. Revelation 11:1 commands the measuring of God’s temple with a reed rather than a cord.

Luke 21:24 says “Jerusalem will be trampled by nations” until the times of nations are fulfilled. Revelation 11:2 says the nations “will trample the holy city” for forty-two months. Revelation does not name the city here.
Revelation 11:3 sets the witnesses’ prophesying at “a thousand two hundred sixty days”. This is a period stated in days next to the “forty-two months” of the trampling in 11:2.

Daniel 7:25 hands the holy ones of the Most High into the oppressor’s power “for a time, times, and half a time”. Revelation 11:2 gives a set period for the holy city to be trampled. Neither text states that the two periods are equal.
Revelation 12:6 uses the same period, “a thousand two hundred sixty days”, for the time the woman is nourished in the wilderness.
Deuteronomy 19:15 requires testimony “At the mouth of two witnesses”. Revelation 11:3 sends exactly “two witnesses”, though Revelation does not cite the legal rule.
Revelation 11:2 gives the nations “forty-two months” to trample the holy city, a period stated in months next to the 1,260 days of the witnesses’ prophesying.

Zechariah asks about “these two olive trees” and is told that they “stand beside the Lord of all the earth”. Revelation 11:4 calls the witnesses “the two olive trees” “standing before the Lord of the earth”.
Zechariah’s vision sets “Two olive trees” beside a golden lampstand. Revelation pairs “two olive trees” with “two lampstands”, where Zechariah has a single lampstand.
Revelation 1:20 explains the lampstands as “seven Churches”. This gives the book’s own key to lampstand imagery, although 11:4 has two lampstands, not seven.
The Lord makes His words “fire in your mouth” to “devour” the people, and the witnesses have fire that “cometh out of their mouth and devoureth their enemies”.

Elijah calls down fire that consumes the men sent against him, and the witnesses destroy those who would harm them with fire. Elijah’s fire comes “down from heaven”, while the witnesses’ fire comes out of their mouth.
Elijah declares there will be “neither dew nor rain” except at his word. The witnesses likewise “have authority to shut heaven, so that rain may not fall” during their prophecy.
Luke 4:25 recalls Elijah’s days “when heaven was shut”, which matches Revelation’s “authority to shut heaven”. Luke gives the drought’s length as three years and six months.

The Philistines recall the gods who “struck Egypt with every plague”. Revelation gives the witnesses power “to strike the earth with every plague”, alongside the Egyptian sign of turning waters into blood.
Revelation 13:7 uses the same sequence, the beast is given “to make war with the saints and conquer them”. In 11:7 the beast does this to the two witnesses.
