Daniel sees a horn “waging war against the holy ones and routing them”. Revelation 11:7 has the beast make war on the witnesses and conquer them. Daniel goes on to the Ancient of Days giving judgment for the holy ones.
Revelation 17:8 describes the beast as “about to come up from the abyss”, the same origin given in 11:7.
Jeremiah says that Jerusalem’s prophets “all became like Sodom to Me”. Revelation calls the great city where the Lord was crucified “spiritually” Sodom. Revelation 11:8 does not name Jerusalem.

Jesus says “it is not possible for a prophet to perish outside Jerusalem”, a city that “kills the prophets”. Revelation sets the prophets’ dead bodies in the city “where also their Lord was crucified”.
Revelation 11:9 continues the scene of 11:8: the peoples look at “their dead body” and do not let it be buried.
Revelation 11:11 picks up the same “three and a half days” and reports the witnesses brought back to life when they are over.
The psalm laments that the “dead bodies” of God’s servants lay exposed and “there was no one to bury them”. Revelation 11:9 says the onlookers “do not allow their dead bodies to be placed in a tomb”.
Revelation 11:5–6 describes the fire, drought and plagues by which the two prophets “tormented those dwelling upon the earth”, the reason for the celebration in 11:10.
Jesus foretells that “the world will rejoice” while His disciples weep. Revelation 11:10 has those dwelling on the earth “rejoice” over the dead witnesses.
Micah tells the enemy, “Do not rejoice over me … because I have fallen! I will rise”. Revelation pictures enemies rejoicing over the fallen prophets, who rise again in 11:11.
Revelation 11:9 sets the period of “three and a half days” during which the dead bodies lie exposed. Revelation 11:11 marks its end.
God breathes into the man “the breath of life” and he becomes a living soul. Revelation 11:11 has “a spirit of life from God” enter the dead witnesses so that they stand.
Jesus is lifted up “as they watched, and a cloud took Him”. The witnesses go up into heaven “in the cloud, and their enemies watched them”.
In both verses a heavenly voice calls, “Come up hither” or “Come up here”. In 4:1 the seer is summoned; in 11:12 the two witnesses are.

Elijah is “taken up … as into heaven” while Elisha looks on, and the witnesses likewise go up into heaven in sight of others. Elijah is taken up in a tumult, with a chariot of fire, rather than in a cloud.
Revelation 14:7 calls people to “Fear God and give Him glory”. This is the response recorded of the survivors in 11:13, who “became fearful and gave glory to the God of heaven”.
In Revelation 16:9–11 people “did not repent to give Him glory” and blasphemed “the God of heaven”. In 11:13 the survivors do give glory to the God of heaven.
Both passages report “a great earthquake” that brings down part of a city. In 11:13 a tenth of the city falls; in 16:18–19 the great city splits into three parts.
Revelation 9:12 uses the same formula for the first woe, “The one woe hath passed. Behold …”. Revelation 11:14 continues the count to the second and third woes.
The eagle’s “Woe, woe, woe” in 8:13 announces the three woes connected with the remaining trumpets. Revelation 11:14 marks the second as passed and the third as coming.
Revelation 10:7 says the mystery of God will be completed “in the days of the voice of the seventh angel”. In 11:15 “the seventh angel sounded” and heaven proclaims the kingdom.
Both proclamations are loud voices in heaven announcing “the kingdom” of God together with His Christ: “the kingdom of our God and the authority of His Christ” in 12:10.
Daniel’s figure receives a kingdom that “will never be destroyed” and an everlasting authority. Revelation proclaims that the Lord and His Christ “will reign for the ages of the ages”.
Revelation 4:4 introduces “twenty-four elders sitting” upon “twenty-four thrones” around the throne. Revelation 11:16 refers back to them in the same terms.
Revelation 19:4 likewise says that “the twenty-four elders … fell and worshipped God”, in response to a heavenly announcement.
Revelation 7:11 uses the same words, “fell upon their faces … and worshipped God”, for the angels around the throne.
Revelation 19:6 proclaims that “the Lord God Almighty hath reigned”. This is the same title and the same claim as the elders’ thanksgiving in 11:17.
Revelation 16:5 addresses God as “the One who is and who was”, the same shortened form as 11:17, without “who is coming”.
Revelation 1:8 combines “the Lord God”, “the One who is and who was” and “the Almighty”. In the fuller form it adds “who is coming”, which 11:17 leaves out.
Revelation 20:12 shows the scene announced in 11:18: “the dead, the great and the small” are judged before the throne.
Revelation 19:5 addresses God’s “slaves and those who fear Him, the small and the great”. This is nearly the same grouping as those who receive the reward in 11:18.
In 22:12 Christ says, “My reward is with Me, to repay each according to what his work is.” This echoes 11:18’s announcement of the time “to give the reward”.
Revelation 8:5 closes the seventh seal with “thunders and voices and lightnings and an earthquake”, and 11:19 closes the seventh trumpet with the same group, adding great hail.
Revelation 16:18 has “lightnings and voices and thunders” and “a great earthquake” at the seventh bowl. Great hail follows in 16:21, giving the same set of signs as 11:19.
Exodus 25:21–22 describes “the ark of the testimony”, from above which God will make Himself known and speak. Revelation 11:19 shows “the ark of His covenant” seen in God’s temple in heaven.
Revelation 12:3 introduces “another sign … in heaven”, the dragon, as a counterpart to the “great sign” of the woman in 12:1.
Revelation 15:1 uses similar language for “another sign in heaven, great and marvellous”, the seven angels with the last plagues.

The Song describes a woman “beautiful like the moon, chosen like the sun”. Revelation’s woman is clothed with the sun with the moon under her feet. The Song uses the sun and moon as comparisons, not as clothing or footstool.

Isaiah speaks of a woman in labor who “bore a male” and of Zion who “labored and bore her children”; Revelation’s woman likewise “crieth out in labour and torment to give birth.” Isaiah stresses a birth before the pains, while Revelation dwells on the torment.
Micah refers to “the time of the woman giving birth”, after which the scattered brothers return. Revelation 12:2 shows a woman in the moment of giving birth. Micah does not describe her pain.
Jesus speaks of a woman giving birth who has “sorrow” and “anguish” until the child is born. Revelation 12:2 describes her “labour and torment to give birth”.
Revelation 12:9 identifies “the great dragon” as “the ancient serpent, who is called the Devil and Satan”.
The beast in 17:7 also has “the seven heads and the ten horns”, the same features given to the dragon in 12:3.
Daniel’s fourth beast has “ten horns upon its head”, matching the dragon’s ten horns. Daniel’s beast has ten horns but no seven heads or diadems.
Revelation 12:2–3 introduces the woman in labour and the great fiery red dragon who stand facing each other in 12:4.
Pharaoh orders that Hebrew male children be killed as the women are “about to give birth”. The dragon waits before the woman “about to give birth” to devour her child.

Daniel’s horn is “raised as high as heaven’s stars” and then dashed to the earth, much as the dragon’s tail throws “a third of the stars of heaven” to the earth. In the Daniel text shown it is the horn, not the stars, that is dashed to the earth.
Psalm 2:9 says “You will shepherd them with an iron rod”. Revelation 12:5 applies this to the male child “who is to shepherd all the nations with an iron rod”.
Revelation 19:15 says of the rider on the white horse, “He will shepherd them with an iron rod”, using the same phrase from the Psalm as 12:5.
Mark records that the Lord Jesus “was taken up into heaven and sat at the right of God”. Revelation’s child “was caught up to God and to His throne”. Revelation 12:5 does not name the child.
Revelation 12:14 retells the woman’s flight “into the wilderness to her place, where she is nourished”. There the period is given as “a time and times and half a time” instead of 1,260 days.
Revelation 11:3 uses the same “thousand two hundred sixty days” for the prophesying of the two witnesses, and 11:2 has forty-two months.

Elijah goes “into the wilderness” and is fed there by the Lord’s angel. The woman flees into the wilderness to a place where she is nourished. Elijah’s flight is not tied to a set number of days, except the later forty days’ journey.

Jude calls Michael “the archangel” and describes him “contending with the devil”. Revelation shows Michael and his angels waging war with the dragon, who is identified in 12:9 as the Devil. Jude’s dispute is over the body of Moses.
Daniel 10:13 shows “Michael, one of the foremost rulers” coming to help against a hostile power. Revelation 12:7 likewise shows Michael in conflict, here against the dragon in heaven.
Daniel 12:1 calls Michael “the great angel who stands over the sons of your people” in a time of great affliction. This is the same angel who leads the heavenly war in Revelation 12:7.
The psalm says of the sinner, “you will seek his place and certainly not find it”. Revelation says of the dragon and his angels that no “place” was “found for them any more in heaven”.
Revelation 12:11 says the brothers “conquered him” by the blood of the Lamb. This is a further statement of the dragon’s defeat reported in 12:8.
Jesus says, “I was watching Satan fall from heaven”. Revelation 12:9 shows Satan “thrown down” to the earth after the war in heaven.

Genesis 3:1 introduces “the serpent” who deceives the woman. Revelation identifies the dragon as “the ancient serpent” and “the one deceiving the whole inhabited world”. Genesis does not itself name the serpent as the Devil.
Revelation 20:10 completes the dragon’s fall: “the devil who deceived them” is thrown into the lake of fire. The verb “thrown” and the role of deceiver are the same as in 12:9.

In both verses voices in heaven announce “the kingdom” of “our God”/“our Lord” together with “His Christ.” Revelation 11:15 speaks of the kingdom of the world becoming His, while 12:10 links the arrival of the kingdom to the accuser being thrown down.

Zechariah sees “the slanderer” standing beside Joshua the high priest “to oppose him” before the angel of the Lord, as Revelation describes one “accusing them before our God.” Zechariah ends with the Lord’s rebuke of the slanderer rather than his being thrown down.

Job shows “the devil” speaking “before the Lord” to cast doubt on a righteous man’s devotion, matching the picture of an accuser of the faithful before God. Job does not describe the accuser being cast down.

Both describe faithful people who die for their witness: “the word of their testimony” and “did not love their life until death” in 12:11, those “beheaded because of the testimony of Jesus and because of the word of God” in 20:4. Revelation 20:4 adds that they lived and reigned with Christ.

Paul says “I consider my life of no value to myself” for the sake of bearing “solemn witness,” close to the conquerors who “did not love their life until death” because of their testimony. Paul speaks of his own ministry, not of a conflict with the accuser.
Both pronounce “Woe” on the earth’s inhabitants in view of coming disaster: an eagle’s threefold woe because of the remaining trumpets, and in 12:12 because “the devil came down to you.”
Isaiah opens with the same summons, “Rejoice, heavens,” grounded in God’s saving act for Israel. Isaiah calls the earth to rejoice as well, whereas Revelation pronounces woe on the earth and the sea.
Isaiah begins “Rejoice, heavens,” giving the reason that God had mercy on His people. Unlike Revelation, Isaiah calls the earth to exult rather than announcing woe upon it.

Revelation 12:3–5 introduces the dragon standing before the woman to devour her child and records that “she bore a son, a male.” Verse 13 resumes that scene: the dragon now pursues “the woman who bore the male child.”

Genesis announces enmity between the one addressed and “the woman,” and between their seeds, as Revelation shows hostility directed at “the woman” and her child. The Genesis verse as shown does not name the addressee; Revelation calls the dragon a serpent elsewhere in the chapter.

Revelation 12:6 already reports the woman fleeing “into the wilderness” to a “place” where she is nourished. Verse 14 repeats the scene, giving the period as “a time and times and half a time” rather than “a thousand two hundred sixty days.”

God says He bore Israel “as upon eagles’ wings” after dealing with the Egyptians, as the woman is given “the two wings of the great eagle” to escape. Exodus uses the wings as a figure of God’s carrying His people, not as a gift of wings to fly into the wilderness.

Daniel gives the same period, “a time, times, and half a time,” for which the holy ones are handed over to the persecuting figure. Revelation uses it for the time the woman is nourished away from the serpent.

Isaiah pictures “the river’s strong and abundant water” brought up against a people to overrun them, as the serpent sends water “like a river” to sweep the woman away. In Isaiah the Lord brings the river and identifies it as the king of the Assyrians.

The psalmist describes “torrents of lawlessness” that threw him into turmoil, the same image of a hostile flood threatening the righteous. The psalm does not describe the water coming from a serpent’s mouth.

Both say that “the earth opened its mouth and swallowed.” In Numbers the earth swallows Korah’s company in judgment; in Revelation it swallows the river the dragon sends against the woman, so the earth acts to rescue.

Deuteronomy recalls “when the earth opened her mouth and swallowed” Dathan and Abiram; Revelation uses the same image of the earth opening its mouth to swallow, here to protect the woman rather than to punish rebels.
Both describe the saints as “those keeping the commandments of God,” paired with a reference to Jesus. Revelation 14:12 has “the faith of Jesus” where 12:17 has “the testimony of Jesus.”
Revelation 19:10 speaks of the brothers “who hold the testimony of Jesus,” the same description given to the woman’s offspring “holding the testimony of Jesus.”
Genesis announces enmity with “the woman” and “her seed,” as the dragon, enraged at the woman, makes war with “the rest of her offspring.” The Genesis verse as shown does not name the one addressed.
The dragon takes his stand “upon the sand of the sea,” and the next verse sees “a beast coming up from the sea.” 13:2 confirms the link: the dragon gives this beast his power and throne.
Both visions see beasts rising out of the sea: Daniel’s “four beasts came up from the sea,” and John’s “beast coming up from the sea.” Daniel sees four distinct beasts; Revelation describes one.
Daniel’s fourth beast “had ten horns,” as does the beast John sees. Daniel’s beast has iron teeth and no seven heads; the ten horns are the specific shared feature.

The dragon of 12:3 has “seven heads and ten horns” with diadems, and the beast from the sea has the same “ten horns and seven heads,” its diadems on the horns rather than the heads. 13:2 then says the dragon gives the beast his power.
Revelation 13:4 restates the transfer: worship is given to the dragon “because he gave authority to the beast,” echoing “the dragon gave it his power and his throne and great authority.”
Revelation 12:9 identifies “the great dragon” as “the ancient serpent, who is called the Devil and Satan,” naming who gives the beast its power and authority in 13:2.
The throne the dragon gives the beast reappears as “the beast’s throne,” on which the fifth bowl is poured, darkening its kingdom.
Revelation 13:12 refers back to “the first beast … whose wound of death was healed,” repeating the phrase from 13:3 and connecting it with the earth worshipping the beast.
Revelation 13:14 describes the same beast as the one “that hath the sword wound and lived,” and specifies that the deadly wound was from a sword.

Both say the earth’s inhabitants “marvel” at the beast. Revelation 17:8 adds that these are people whose names are not written in the book of life and that the beast “was and is not and will be present.”
Revelation 13:2 narrates what 13:4 summarises: “the dragon gave it his power and his throne and great authority.”
The acclamation “Who is like the beast?” uses the form of Moses’ song, “Who is like Thee among the gods, O Lord?” Revelation applies to the beast the praise that Exodus gives to the Lord.
The worshippers ask, “who is able to wage war with it?”; Revelation 17:14 says that the beast’s allies “will wage war with the Lamb, and the Lamb will conquer them.”
Daniel’s little horn has “a mouth speaking great things,” the same phrase used for the beast’s mouth. Daniel’s horn sprouts on the fourth beast; in Revelation the mouth is given to the beast itself.

Daniel’s figure “will speak words against the Most High” and is given power “for a time, times, and half a time,” paralleling the beast’s blasphemies and its limited “forty-two months.” The two periods are expressed differently in the two texts.
Daniel’s king “will speak extraordinary things against the God of gods” and prosper for a set time, as the beast is given a mouth for “blasphemies” and authority for a fixed period.

Revelation 12:12 calls on the “heavens and those dwelling in them” to rejoice, while in 13:6 the beast blasphemes “those dwelling in heaven.” Both concern those in heaven, beyond the reach of the dragon’s fury on earth.

The beast blasphemes God’s “tent,” and Revelation 21:3 announces “the tabernacle of God” dwelling with men. The Saints texts use “tent” and “tabernacle” for these, and 21:3 places God’s dwelling among people rather than in heaven.
Daniel sees the horn “waging war against the holy ones and routing them,” closely matching “to make war with the saints and conquer them.” Daniel attributes this to a horn on the fourth beast.
Revelation 11:7 uses the same sequence for the beast from the abyss: it “will make war with them and conquer them,” there directed at the two witnesses.
Both use the fourfold formula “every tribe and … tongue and people and nation.” In 5:9 the Lamb purchases people from them for God; in 13:7 the beast receives authority over them.

Revelation 17:8 repeats that “those dwelling upon the earth, whose name hath not been written in the book of life from the foundation of the world” respond to the beast, there by marvelling rather than worshipping.
Both speak of the book of life as belonging to the Lamb, “the Lamb’s book of life” in 21:27. There those written in it enter the city; in 13:8 those not written in it worship the beast.
Peter speaks of the blood of Christ “as of a lamb” who was foreknown “before the foundation of the world,” connecting the slaughtered Lamb with the foundation of the world as 13:8 does.

The call “Let the one who hath an ear hear” in the letters to the churches is echoed in “If anyone hath an ear, let him hear.” Here the formula lacks the words “what the Spirit saith to the Churches.”
Revelation 2:29 gives the hearing formula on its own, “Let the one who hath an ear hear,” which 13:9 adapts as “If anyone hath an ear, let him hear.”

Jeremiah’s oracle has the same pattern: “as many for sword, to sword … as many for captivity, to captivity.” Jeremiah lists death and famine too and announces judgment, while Revelation applies the pattern to the saints’ endurance.
Jeremiah repeats the formula against Egypt: “those for deportation, to deportation; and those for the sword, to the sword,” the pattern Revelation uses for captivity and the sword.
Revelation 14:12 repeats the closing words, “Here is the endurance of the saints,” adding a description of the saints as keeping God’s commandments and the faith of Jesus.
Revelation 13:1 presents the first beast “coming up from the sea”; 13:11 introduces “another beast coming up from the earth,” and its speech “like a dragon” links it to the dragon of 12:17–18.

Jesus warns of false prophets who come “in sheep’s clothing,” a harmless appearance concealing a threat, much as the beast has horns “like a lamb” yet speaks “like a dragon.” Matthew does not mention horns or a beast.
Revelation 13:3–4 describes the first beast whose “wound of death was healed” and the earth’s worship of it, which the second beast now enforces.

Revelation 19:20 refers to the false prophet who acted “before it,” on behalf of the beast, and to “those worshipping its image.” The same activity on the beast’s behalf is described in 13:12, and 19:20 records the end of both.
The third angel warns, “If anyone worshippeth the beast and its image,” addressing the very worship that 13:12 says the second beast imposes on the earth.

In the Elijah story “fire came down from heaven” and consumed the king’s men, the sign the second beast imitates when it makes “fire come down from heaven to the earth.” Elijah acts as a man of God; the beast performs the sign to deceive.
Revelation 19:20 names the one who “performed the signs before it” as the false prophet, who deceived people by them, the activity 13:13 introduces.
Jesus foretells false prophets who “give great signs and wonders, so as to lead astray,” matching the “great signs” performed by the second beast.
Revelation 19:20 refers back to this deception: the false prophet “performed the signs before it, by which he deceived” those who received the mark and worshipped the image.
Revelation 13:15 continues the account of the image made for the beast: it is given breath, speaks, and causes non-worshippers to be killed.
The dragon is “the one deceiving the whole inhabited world,” and the second beast likewise “deceiveth those dwelling upon the earth,” carrying on the dragon’s deception.

Nebuchadnezzar orders the nations to “bow to the golden image” and decrees death in the furnace for anyone who does not, as the beast’s image causes those who “would not worship the beast’s image” to be killed.
Revelation 20:4 includes among those enthroned “those who did not worship the beast or its image,” the faithful against whom the image’s death decree was directed.
The third angel warns against anyone who “worshippeth the beast and its image,” the worship the image enforces on pain of death.
In Ezekiel a “sign” is put “upon the foreheads” of those grieving over Jerusalem’s lawlessness, marking them out. Revelation’s mark identifies the beast’s followers, not the faithful.
God’s slaves are sealed “upon their foreheads” in 7:3, the counterpart to the beast’s mark “upon their right hand or upon their forehead.”
The third angel warns that anyone who receives “a mark upon his forehead or upon his hand” will drink the wine of God’s fury, the same mark that 13:16 says is imposed.
Revelation 13:18 continues by inviting the reader to calculate “the number of the beast,” explaining the “number of its name” mentioned in 13:17.
Revelation 15:2 lists “the beast and its image and the number of its name” as what the victors conquered, using the same phrase “the number of its name.”
Revelation 14:11 speaks of “anyone who receiveth the mark of its name,” combining mark and name as 13:17 does, and describes the torment that awaits them.
Revelation 17:9 uses a similar call to discernment, “Here is the mind that hath wisdom,” before explaining the beast’s heads, as 13:18 says “Here is wisdom” before the number of the beast.
Revelation 21:17 calls the wall’s measure “a human measure,” a phrase like the “human number” of 13:18. The context is the city’s wall, not the beast.
Revelation 15:2 mentions those who conquered “the number of its name,” the number that 13:18 asks the reader to calculate.
Christ promises to write on the conqueror “the name of My God” and “My new name”; in 14:1 the hundred forty-four thousand have “His name and His Father’s name written upon their foreheads.”
The psalm’s speaker is appointed king “on Zion, His holy mountain,” the place where the Lamb is seen standing in 14:1.

Joel says that “on Mount Zion and in Jerusalem there will be one who escapes,” a saved remnant on Zion like the company standing with the Lamb. Joel does not give their number or mention names on foreheads.
The voice of the risen Christ is “like the sound of many waters,” the same comparison used for the voice from heaven in 14:2.
Revelation 15:2 shows the victors standing on the glassy sea “having lyres of God,” the instrument heard in 14:2.
One of the living creatures speaks “as with a voice of thunder,” a comparison also used in 14:2, “like the sound of great thunder.”
In 5:9 the heavenly worshippers “sing a new song” to the Lamb who “didst purchase for God” people, matching the “new song” and those “purchased from the earth” in 14:3.
Revelation 14:1 introduces the “hundred forty-four thousand” with the Lamb on Mount Zion, the only ones able to learn the song in 14:3.
The psalm calls, “Sing to the Lord a new song,” because of the salvation His right hand won, the kind of song sung in 14:3. The psalm does not restrict who can learn it.
The scribe promises Jesus, “I will follow Thee wherever Thou goest,” closely matching “following the Lamb wherever He goeth.” Matthew records only an offer to follow, not the outcome.
James says believers were given birth so they might be “a kind of firstfruits of His creatures,” the same image applied to the redeemed as “firstfruits to God and to the Lamb.”
Paul wants to present the church “as a pure virgin to Christ,” comparable to calling the followers of the Lamb “virgins.” Paul uses the image for a whole church betrothed to Christ.
Zephaniah says of the remnant of Israel that “no deceitful tongue will be found in their mouth,” closely paralleling “no lie was found in their mouth.”
Isaiah says of the servant that “nor was deceit found in his mouth,” language applied in 14:5 to the Lamb’s followers.
Paul says Christ will present the church “holy and without blemish,” the same quality ascribed to the redeemed, who “are unblemished.”
Revelation 8:13 likewise has a messenger “flying in midheaven” addressing those on the earth; there an eagle announces woes rather than good news.
Revelation 13:7 lists “every tribe and people and tongue and nation” as under the beast’s authority; in 14:6 the same peoples receive the eternal good news.
Jesus commands, “proclaim the gospel to all creation,” as the angel has “good news to proclaim” to every nation. Mark’s commission is given to the disciples, not to an angel.
The commandment states that “the Lord made heaven and earth and the sea,” the creation formula on which the angel bases his call to worship. Revelation adds “springs of waters.”
Esdras confesses that God made heaven, “the earth and everything in it, the seas,” and that heaven’s armies “worship Thee,” combining creation and worship as 14:7 does.
Revelation 15:4 asks, “Who shall not fear, Lord, and glorify Thy name,” and says the nations “shall come and worship,” matching the angel’s “Fear God and give Him glory … and worship.”
Revelation 18:2–3 repeats nearly word for word: “Fallen, fallen is Babylon the great” and “all the nations have drunk from the wine of the fury of her sexual immorality.”
Isaiah’s watchman reports, “Babylon has fallen,” with her statues shattered, the announcement repeated by the second angel.

Jeremiah describes Babylon as a cup from which “Nations drank her wine,” and says “Suddenly Babylon fell,” combining the fall and the nations’ drinking as in 14:8. Jeremiah calls the cup the Lord’s rather than linking the wine to sexual immorality.
Revelation 14:11 completes the third angel’s warning about “those worshipping the beast and its image, and anyone who receiveth the mark,” describing their unending torment.
Revelation 14:6–8 introduces the first and second angels; 14:9 continues the sequence with “another angel, a third.”

The psalm says “in the Lord’s hand is a cup of unmixed wine” of which “all the earth’s sinners will drink,” matching the wine “prepared unmixed in the cup of His wrath.” The psalm also speaks of mixture and dregs.
The psalm says “fire, sulfur” are “the portion of their cup” for sinners, combining cup, fire and sulfur as 14:10 does.
Revelation 16:19 speaks of “the cup of the wine of the fury of His wrath” given to Babylon, the same wording as in 14:10, applied to the city rather than to individual worshippers.
Isaiah says of Edom’s land that its burning will continue “night and day” and “her smoke will rise upward” for an everlasting time, the image applied to the beast’s worshippers.
Revelation 19:3 says of Babylon, “her smoke goeth up for the ages of the ages,” the same expression used in 14:11.
Revelation 20:10 says the devil, the beast and the false prophet “will be tormented day and night for the ages of the ages,” matching the unceasing torment “day and night” in 14:11.
Revelation 13:10 ends with the same formula, “Here is the endurance and the faith of the saints.”

Revelation 12:17 describes the woman’s offspring as “those keeping the commandments of God and holding the testimony of Jesus,” the same description of the saints with “testimony” in place of “faith.”
Revelation 19:9 has the same command and beatitude form, “Write: Blessed are …,” there for those called to the Lamb’s marriage supper.

Hebrews says the one who entered God’s rest “rested from his own works,” paralleling the dead who “rest from their labours.” Hebrews speaks of a Sabbath rest that remains for God’s people, not explicitly of the dead.
Wisdom says that a righteous person who dies early “will be at rest,” the same rest promised to the dead who die in the Lord.
Daniel sees “upon the clouds of heaven, one like a son of man,” the figure John sees sitting “upon the cloud … like a son of man.” Daniel does not mention a crown or a sickle.
Revelation 1:13 describes “One like a son of man” among the lampstands, using the same title for the figure who appears here with a golden crown and sickle.
Joel calls, “Send out sickles,” where the Lord will sit to judge the nations, the harvest-judgment imagery behind the sickle in the hand of the One on the cloud.

Joel’s command “Send out sickles, because the vintage is at hand” is the pattern for “Send Thy sickle and reap, because the hour to reap hath come.” Joel speaks of the vintage and winepress, which Revelation takes up in 14:18–20.

In the parable the farmer “sends in the sickle, because the harvest has arrived,” using the same sequence of sickle and ripe harvest. The parable concerns the growth of the kingdom rather than judgment.
Jesus explains that “the harvest is the consummation of the age” and “the reapers are angels,” the end-time harvest image in which an angel here calls for the reaping.
Revelation 14:14 introduces the “One sitting upon the cloud” holding “a sharp sickle,” the figure who now casts the sickle on the earth.
Revelation 14:19 repeats the action with an angel who “cast his sickle into the earth,” this time gathering the vine for the winepress of God’s fury.
Revelation 14:14–15 shows the One on the cloud with “a sharp sickle” and an angel coming “out of the temple”; 14:17 introduces another angel from the temple, “himself also having a sharp sickle.”
Revelation 14:18 addresses this angel as “the one having the sharp sickle” and commands him to gather the clusters of the vine.

Joel’s “Send out sickles, because the vintage is at hand!” lies behind “Send thy sharp sickle and gather the clusters … because its grapes have ripened.” Joel goes on to the trodden winepress, as Revelation does in 14:19–20.

Revelation 14:15–16 has the same pattern: an angel cries “with a loud voice” to the one with the sickle, “Send Thy sickle and reap,” and the earth is reaped. The first harvest is of grain; the second is of the vine.

Deuteronomy speaks of a wicked people’s “vine” as “of the vine of Sodom,” with grapes of gall and a bitter “cluster,” the image of a corrupt vine taken up in “the vine of the earth.” Deuteronomy describes the vine’s fruit, not its harvest or a winepress.

In Isaiah the Lord’s garments are red as from “a trodden winepress”: He trampled the nations “in wrath” and “brought their blood down to earth.” This is the image of a winepress of judgment yielding blood, as in 14:20.
Lamentations says “The Lord trod a winepress” against Daughter Judah, using the treading of the winepress as a picture of God’s judgment. There it falls on Judah, not on the nations.
Revelation 15:6–7 continues the vision: “the seven angels having the seven plagues” come out of the temple and receive “seven golden bowls full of the fury of God.”
Revelation 21:9 refers back to “the seven angels having the seven bowls full of the seven last plagues,” repeating the description from 15:1.
God warns that He will “add seven blows” upon those who will not obey, the sevenfold stroke of judgment that Revelation presents as seven plagues.
Revelation 4:6 first shows “something like a glassy sea” before the throne; 15:2 sees it again, now “mixed with fire” with the victors standing on it.
In 5:8 the living creatures and elders each hold “a lyre” in worship before the Lamb, as the victors in 15:2 hold “lyres of God.”
The psalm says, “Great are the works of the Lord,” echoed in the song “Great and marvellous are Thy works.”
The psalm says “The Lord is righteous in all His ways,” matching “righteous and true are Thy ways.”
The psalmist says “wondrous are Thy works,” paralleling “marvellous are Thy works.” The psalm praises God for how the speaker was made.

The psalm says, “All the nations Thou madest will come and bow down before Thee, Lord, and glorify Thy name,” which the song closely reproduces: “glorify Thy name … all the nations shall come and worship before Thee.”
The first angel calls, “Fear God and give Him glory … and worship,” the response that 15:4 says the nations will finally give.
Malachi says the Lord’s name “has been glorified among the nations” and is great among them, matching the expectation that all nations will glorify His name.
Both verses describe the temple in heaven being “opened.” In 11:19 the ark of His covenant is then seen; here the opening leads to the coming out of the seven angels with the seven plagues.

Revelation calls the heavenly sanctuary “the temple of the tent of the testimony,” using the same title Numbers gives the wilderness “Tent of Testimony” served by the Levites. Numbers speaks of the earthly tent and its furnishings, not a temple in heaven.

The angels are “girded around their chests with golden belts,” as the One like a son of man is “girded around the chest with a golden belt.” The angels wear pure, bright linen, whereas the son of man wears a robe reaching to the feet.
Both verses speak of the “seven angels having seven plagues.” 15:1 introduces them as a sign in heaven; 15:6 shows them coming out of the temple.

Both verses speak of the seven angels with seven bowls full of judgement: here “seven golden bowls full of the fury of God,” there “the seven bowls full of the seven last plagues.” In 21:9 one of these angels shows John the bride.
Both scenes pair the four living creatures with “golden bowls full of” something. In 5:8 the bowls are full of incense, “the prayers of the saints,” whereas here they are full of “the fury of God.”

The throne vision introduces the four living creatures and describes God as “the One living for the ages of the ages”; 15:7 uses the same description of God and has one of the four living creatures hand over the bowls.

In both, the sanctuary is filled with the glory of God and no one can go in: “Moses could not enter the Tent of Testimony” because the tent “was filled with the glory of the Lord.” Exodus speaks of a cloud; Revelation speaks of smoke and adds that entry is barred until the seven plagues are completed.

In both visions the sanctuary is filled with smoke: “the house was filled with smoke” and “the temple was filled with smoke.” Isaiah links the smoke to the seraphim’s cry, while Revelation links it to the glory and power of God.

At the temple’s dedication the Lord’s glory filled the house and the priests “could not stand to minister,” just as in Revelation no one could enter the temple. Kings speaks of a cloud rather than smoke.
The voice sends out the seven angels who in 15:5–8 came out of the temple and received “seven golden bowls full of the fury of God.” 16:1 orders that these bowls now be poured out on the earth.
The bowl sequence opens and closes with “a loud voice” from the temple. In 16:1 it orders the bowls poured out; in 16:17, after the seventh bowl, it declares “It hath happened.”

Jeremiah prays, “Pour Thy fury upon nations,” and Revelation commands the angels to “pour out the seven bowls of God’s fury into the earth.” Jeremiah asks this against nations that devoured Jacob, while Revelation’s command extends to the earth.

Like the Egyptian plague in which boils broke out “on people,” the first bowl brings a painful sore upon people. In Exodus the boils come from scattered furnace soot and fall on Egypt’s people and animals, while in Revelation the sore falls on those bearing the beast’s mark.
The sores of the first bowl are mentioned again after the fifth, when people blaspheme God “because of their pains and their sores” and do not repent.
The sore falls on “the people having the mark of the beast and worshipping its image,” the people described in 13:15–17, where the beast’s image is worshipped and all are made to receive the mark.

The second trumpet and the second bowl both strike the sea: it “became blood” and creatures in the sea died. The trumpet affects a third of the sea and its creatures, while the bowl kills “every living soul” in the sea.

Water turned to blood and the death of the creatures in it recall the Egyptian plague, where “all the water in the river turned to blood” and “the fish in the river died.” Exodus concerns Egypt’s river and waters, while Revelation concerns the sea.
The psalm summarises the Egyptian plague: “He turned their waters into blood and killed their fish,” the same pairing of blood and death of water creatures found in the second bowl.
As in Egypt, where the waters over “their rivers” were to “become blood,” the third bowl turns the rivers and springs to blood. Exodus is limited to the waters of Egypt.

The third trumpet and the third bowl both fall on “the rivers and … the springs of the waters.” The trumpet affects a third of them and makes them bitter as wormwood, whereas the bowl turns them to blood.
The next verse continues the scene: “the angel of the waters” declares God righteous for judging “these things,” meaning the waters turned to blood.

Both address God as “the One who is and who was” without the further phrase “who is coming” used in 1:4, 1:8 and 4:8. In 11:17 the elders give thanks for His reign; here the angel praises His judgment.
The angel’s confession that God is righteous in His judging is echoed at once by the altar: “true and righteous are Thy judgments.”

The psalm pairs the same attributes, calling the Lord “righteous in all His ways and holy in all His works,” as the angel calls God “righteous” and “the Holy One.” The psalm states this generally, while Revelation applies it to a specific judgment.
Both verses speak of the blood of “saints and prophets” (18:24: “prophets and saints”). 18:24 locates that blood in Babylon, while 16:6 speaks of those who poured it out being given blood to drink.

In both, God makes oppressors drink blood as punishment: “drink their own blood like new wine” and “given them blood to drink.” Isaiah’s oppressors afflicted Jacob, while Revelation’s shed the blood of saints and prophets.

The souls under the altar ask how long before God will “judge and avenge our blood upon those dwelling on the earth.” 16:6 describes God giving blood to drink to those who poured out the blood of saints.
Both use the same praise of God’s judgments: “true and righteous are Thy judgments” and “His judgments are true and righteous.” 19:2 applies it to the judgment of the great prostitute.

The song of Moses and of the Lamb also addresses the “Lord God Almighty” and confesses “righteous and true are Thy ways.” The song praises God’s ways and works generally, while 16:7 speaks of His judgments.
The altar speaks here, and in 6:9 the altar is where the souls of those slaughtered for the word of God were seen. 16:7 does not itself identify the speaker beyond “the altar.”
The fourth trumpet and the fourth bowl both affect the sun. The trumpet darkens a third of the sun, while the bowl makes the sun “scorch people with fire.”
Those standing before the throne are promised that the sun will not fall upon them, “nor any burning heat,” whereas under the fourth bowl the sun is given power to scorch people with fire.
After the fifth bowl the same reaction is repeated: people “blasphemed the God of heaven” and “did not repent.” Here the cause is great heat; there it is pains and sores.

After the trumpet plagues the survivors likewise “did not even repent,” as people under the fourth bowl “did not repent.” In 9:20 the unrepented sins are named as idolatry; 16:9 adds blasphemy of God’s name.
The angel calls all to “Fear God and give Him glory,” and the scorched people refuse to “give Him glory.” 14:7 is a summons; 16:9 records its refusal.

As the ninth Egyptian plague brought darkness on Pharaoh’s land, the fifth bowl darkens the beast’s kingdom. Exodus specifies three days of darkness and light for Israel, details Revelation does not give.
The bowl is poured on “the beast’s throne,” the throne the dragon gave to the beast in 13:2 along with his power and great authority.
The fourth and fifth bowls end alike: people blaspheme God and do not repent. 16:9 adds that they refuse “to give Him glory.”
The “sores” for which people blaspheme recall the “bad and painful sore” of the first bowl, which came upon those having the mark of the beast.
Both verses use the title “the God of heaven.” After the earthquake in 11:13 the survivors “gave glory to the God of heaven,” whereas here people blaspheme Him and do not repent.
The sixth trumpet and the sixth bowl both centre on “the great river Euphrates.” In 9:14 four angels bound there are loosed; here its water is dried up.

Isaiah describes the Lord bringing His hand upon “the river” so “that one may pass through it in sandals,” as the Euphrates is dried so that a way may be prepared. Isaiah’s passage serves a returning people, Revelation’s the kings from the east.
Isaiah speaks of one roused “from the sun’s rising,” as Revelation speaks of “the kings from the rising of the sun.” Isaiah does not mention the drying of a river.
The next verse explains the three frog-like spirits: they are “spirits of demons performing signs” who go out to gather the kings for war.
The beast and the false prophet named here appear together again at their capture, where the false prophet is described as performing signs and deceiving, and both are thrown into the lake of fire.
Frogs recall the Egyptian plague, when the land “teemed with frogs in the chambers of their kings.” In Revelation the frogs are an image for unclean spirits, not a literal plague.
The gathering for war announced here is carried out two verses later: “they gathered them to the place called in Hebrew Harmagedon.”
In both, a deceiving power goes out “to gather them for war” on a worldwide scale. In 20:8 it is Satan gathering Gog and Magog after the thousand years, whereas here demonic spirits gather the kings.
Both name the coming judgment as “the great day”: “the great day of Their wrath” and “the great day of God Almighty.”
The warning to Sardis uses the same words: “I will come like a thief,” with a call to watch, and then speaks of those who “did not defile their garments.”
The counsel to Laodicea to buy white garments so “the shame of thy nakedness may not be manifested” matches the blessing on keeping one’s garments so as not to walk naked and have one’s shame seen.

Jesus’ call to “keep watch” because the householder does not know when “the thief was coming” lies behind the blessing on the one who “watcheth.” Matthew uses a parable of a house broken into, without the image of garments.

Judges describes kings who “drew up in battle” and fought “by Megiddo’s water,” a battle of kings at the place whose name resembles Harmagedon. Revelation gives only the Hebrew name and does not explain it.
King Josiah is killed by Pharaoh Nechao “at Mageddo,” another clash of kings at the place whose name resembles Harmagedon. The connection rests on the similarity of the place-names.
The gathering is completed when the beast, “the kings of the earth and their armies” are “gathered to wage war” against the rider on the horse. 19:19 does not name the place.
The bowl sequence that began with “a loud voice from the temple” ends with “a loud voice” coming “out of the temple from the throne.”
Both are short divine declarations of completion: “It hath happened” and “They have come to be.” 16:17 closes the bowl judgments, while 21:6 refers to the making of all things new.

At the seventh trumpet, as at the seventh bowl, the final element of the series is followed by loud voices in heaven. The trumpet voices proclaim the kingdom, while the bowl voice says “It hath happened.”
Both describe “lightnings and voices and thunders” with an earthquake at the close of a series of seven, and both include great hail (16:21). 16:18 stresses that this earthquake is unmatched.

Daniel’s day of affliction “such as has not occurred since they came into being” has the same unmatched-in-history formula as the earthquake “such as had not occurred since human beings came to be upon the earth.” Daniel speaks of affliction, not an earthquake.
The same cluster of “thunders and voices and lightnings and an earthquake” follows the angel’s censer being thrown to earth before the trumpets.
Babylon being “remembered before God” is restated in 18:5: “God remembered her wrongdoings.”
18:10 identifies “the great city” as “Babylon, the mighty city,” matching the pairing here of “the great city” with “Babylon the great,” and announces that her judgment came.
The judgment on “Babylon the great” announced here is proclaimed as accomplished in 18:2: “Fallen, fallen is Babylon the great.”
At the sixth seal “every mountain and island were moved from their places,” as at the seventh bowl “every island fled, and mountains were not found.”
Before the great white throne earth and heaven “fled, and no place was found for them,” using the same verbs “fled” and “found” as the islands and mountains here.
The seventh trumpet sequence ends with “an earthquake and great hail,” as the seventh bowl brings a great earthquake (16:18) followed by “great hail.”

In both, God sends hail “from heaven” upon His enemies with deadly effect. In Joshua the hail falls on fleeing armies; in Revelation the hail, about a talent in weight, falls on people who then blaspheme God.
God’s judgment on Gog includes “hailstones,” as the final bowl brings great hail. Ezekiel also lists fire and sulfur, which Revelation does not mention here.

Both visions are introduced in nearly the same words: one of the seven angels having the seven bowls “came and spoke with me, saying, ‘Come, I will show thee.’” Here the angel shows the great prostitute; in 21:9 he shows the bride, the wife of the Lamb.
The “judgment of the great prostitute” promised here is celebrated as accomplished in 19:2: God “judged the great prostitute.”
Jeremiah addresses those “who dwell beside many waters” and announces their end, as the prostitute is “sitting upon many waters.” The verse shown does not itself name the one addressed.
18:3 repeats the charge almost word for word: “the kings of the earth committed sexual immorality with her,” and the nations drank “the wine of the fury of her sexual immorality.”
The second angel’s announcement already speaks of Babylon making “all the nations drink from the wine of the fury of her sexual immorality.”
Jeremiah portrays Babylon as a cup “making the whole earth drunk,” and “Nations drank her wine,” as the earth’s inhabitants became drunk from her wine. Jeremiah does not speak of sexual immorality.
The two contrasting visions open alike: “he carried me away in the Spirit.” Here John is taken into a wilderness to see the prostitute; in 21:10 to a great and high mountain to see the holy city.
The scarlet beast has “seven heads and ten horns,” as does the great fiery red dragon. The dragon also has seven diadems, and the beast is full of names of blasphemy.
Daniel’s beast has “ten horns upon its head” and a horn “speaking great things,” as the beast here has ten horns and is full of names of blasphemy. Daniel’s beast has ten horns but no seven heads.
The great city is lamented as “clothed in fine linen and purple and scarlet and adorned with gold and precious stone and pearl,” nearly the same description given of the woman.
Jeremiah calls Babylon “a golden cup” from which the nations drank, as the woman holds “a golden cup.” In Jeremiah the cup is in the Lord’s hand; here it is in hers and full of abominations.
The woman’s cup reappears in the call for judgment: “in the cup in which she mixed, mix a double portion for her.”
The name on her forehead is called “a mystery,” and the angel then promises to explain “the mystery of the woman.”
The name “Babylon the great” first appears in the second angel’s cry, “Fallen, fallen is Babylon the great,” where she makes the nations drink the wine of her sexual immorality.
The fall of “Babylon the great” is announced in the same words in 18:2, where she is described as a dwelling of demons and unclean things.
The charge is repeated at Babylon’s fall: “in her was found blood of prophets and saints.” 18:24 adds “all those slaughtered upon the earth.”
Both speak of the “blood of saints” and of drinking blood. In 17:6 the woman is drunk with the saints’ blood; in 16:6 God gives those who shed it blood to drink as punishment.
Antipas is called “My witness, My faithful one, who was killed,” an example of the “witnesses of Jesus” whose blood the woman drinks. 2:13 names Satan’s throne, not the woman, as the setting.
The “mystery of the woman and of the beast” refers back to the vision of 17:1–6, where the woman sits upon a scarlet beast with seven heads and ten horns and John marvels at her.
The explanation promised here begins in the next verse with the beast that “was and is not,” at which those dwelling on the earth “will marvel.”
17:11 repeats the description of “the beast that was and is not” and that “goeth into destruction,” adding that it is an eighth and from the seven.
Both describe “the beast coming up from the abyss.” In 11:7 it makes war on the two witnesses and kills them.
Those whose names are not written “in the book of life” marvel at the beast here, and in 20:15 anyone “not found written in the book of life” is thrown into the lake of fire.
Both open an interpretive riddle about the beast with a call to wisdom: “Here is wisdom” and “Here is the mind that hath wisdom.” 13:18 concerns the beast’s number, 17:9 its seven heads.
The seven heads explained here are those of the scarlet beast on which the woman was seen sitting in 17:3.
The angel had promised to explain the mystery of the beast “which hath the seven heads and the ten horns”; 17:9 begins that explanation with the heads.
17:9 identifies the beast’s seven heads as “seven kings”; 17:10 continues that interpretation, counting five who “fell,” one who “is,” and one not yet come.
After the seven kings of 17:10, the beast itself is called “an eighth” that “is from the seven,” completing the same count.
17:11 restates 17:8: the beast “was and is not” and “goeth into destruction.” 17:11 adds that it is an eighth and is from the seven.

Daniel interprets the beast’s horns in the same way: “ten horns, ten kings will arise.” Daniel adds another king who humbles three, while Revelation says the ten receive authority “for one hour with the beast.”
The beast from the sea has “ten horns,” with ten diadems on them, as here the beast’s “ten horns” are ten kings. 13:1 does not interpret the horns.
The same “ten horns thou sawest” later turn with the beast against the prostitute and make her desolate.
17:17 repeats that the kings “do one purpose and give their kingdom to the beast,” and adds that God put it into their hearts to do His purpose.
Deuteronomy calls the Lord God “God of gods and Lord of lords,” a title Revelation gives to the Lamb as “Lord of lords and King of kings.”
Paul calls God “the King of those who reign and Lord of those who rule,” the same pairing of kingship and lordship over rulers as “Lord of lords and King of kings.” The wording differs.

Those with the Lamb are “called and chosen and faithful,” using the two terms of Jesus’ saying “many are called, but few chosen.” Matthew distinguishes the called from the chosen; Revelation applies both to the same group.
The waters explained here are the “many waters” on which the great prostitute was said to sit in 17:1.
The beast is given authority over “every tribe and people and tongue and nation,” a list closely matching “peoples and multitudes and nations and tongues” here.
Jeremiah addresses those “who dwell beside many waters,” the image Revelation interprets as peoples and nations. The verse shown does not itself name the one addressed.
The burning of the prostitute is announced again in 18:8: “she will be burned up with fire.” 18:8 attributes the judgment to the Lord God, while 17:16 names the ten horns and the beast as its agents.
The desolation of the prostitute is lamented in 18:19: “in one hour she was made desolate!”

Ezekiel describes adulteresses punished by a gathered multitude who kill and “burn their houses,” as the beast and the horns turn on the prostitute and burn her. Ezekiel speaks of stoning and swords, not of eating her flesh.
17:13 had said the kings “have one purpose, and give their power and authority to the beast”; 17:17 explains that God put this purpose into their hearts.

Ezra blesses the Lord “who put it thus in the king’s heart,” as Revelation says “God put it into their hearts to do His purpose.” In Ezra the purpose is to glorify the Lord’s house, here to give their kingdom to the beast.
Both speak of what God has announced being “completed”: “the mystery of God will be completed” and “until the words of God are completed.”
The woman is identified as “the great city,” and in 16:19 “the great city” is spoken of together with “Babylon the great.”
In Ezekiel “the earth flashed like radiance from the glory,” and here “the earth was illuminated from his glory.” In Ezekiel the glory is the God of Israel’s; here it belongs to an angel.
Both introduce another angel “coming down from heaven”: in 10:1 a mighty angel with his face like the sun, here one with great authority whose glory lights the earth.
The same cry, “Fallen, fallen is Babylon the great,” was first announced by the second angel in 14:8.
Jeremiah announces, “Suddenly Babylon fell and was shattered,” as the angel cries that Babylon is “fallen.”
Jeremiah foretells that Babylon “will become a ruin and will not be inhabited,” as here she becomes a haunt of demons and unclean creatures rather than people.
17:2 makes the same charge: “the kings of the earth committed sexual immorality” with her and the earth’s inhabitants became drunk “from the wine of her sexual immorality.”
14:8 uses the same phrase about the nations drinking “from the wine of the fury of her sexual immorality.”
Jeremiah says of Babylon, “Nations drank her wine,” as here “all the nations have drunk from the wine” of Babylon. Jeremiah does not mention sexual immorality or merchants.
Jeremiah urges, “Flee from Babylon’s midst … Do not be cast away in her injustice,” matching the call to come out of her so as not to share in her sins and plagues.
Jeremiah commands, “Separate yourselves from Babylon’s midst … come out,” as the heavenly voice says, “Come out of her, My people.”
Isaiah’s “Go out from her midst; separate yourselves” and “do not touch anything unclean” parallel the call to leave so as not to share her sins. Isaiah does not name Babylon in this verse.
Jeremiah says of Babylon that “her judgment reached heaven,” as here “her sins have piled up as far as heaven.” Jeremiah speaks of her judgment, Revelation of her sins.
“God remembered her wrongdoings” restates 16:19, where Babylon the great “was remembered before God” to receive the cup of His wrath.
Ezra confesses that “our offenses have grown to heaven,” the same picture of sins rising to heaven. Ezra is confessing Israel’s own sins, not announcing judgment on another city.
Jeremiah commands, “Repay her according to her works; do to her all she did,” as Revelation says, “Repay her as she also repaid … according to her works.” Revelation adds a doubled repayment.
The psalm blesses the one “who will repay you the repayment you gave us,” addressing daughter Babylon, as here Babylon is to be repaid as she repaid.
“The cup in which she mixed” is the golden cup full of abominations the woman held in 17:4.

Babylon’s boast in Isaiah, “I will not sit as a widow or know bereavement,” spoken “in her heart,” is closely echoed: “in her heart she saith, ‘I sit a queen, and I am not a widow.’” Isaiah adds that widowhood and childlessness will come “in one day.”
Zephaniah’s city, “saying in her heart, ‘I am, and there is no one after me,’” makes the same kind of self-exalting inner boast as Babylon. Zephaniah does not mention widowhood or queenship.

Both verses describe the woman being burned with fire: “she will be burned up with fire” and “burn her up with fire.” Revelation 17:16 names the beast and the ten horns as the agents, while 18:8 grounds the burning in the Lord God who judged her.

Both oracles against Babylon ground her judgment in the strength of the Lord: “the Lord God who judged her is mighty” and “The One redeeming them is strong; the Lord Almighty is His name. He will judge a case against His adversaries.” Jeremiah speaks of Babylon’s inhabitants; Revelation applies the language to the city pictured as a woman.
Both verses describe onlookers who “see the smoke of her burning” and lament the city. In 18:9 the mourners are the kings of the earth; in 18:18 they are the seafarers.

Both verses say “the kings of the earth committed sexual immorality with her” and associate her with luxury. Revelation 18:3 gives the cause of her judgment; 18:9 shows the same kings mourning her fall.

The merchants repeat the kings’ posture and cry: they “stand far away because of fear of her torment” and say “Woe, woe, the great city … because in one hour.” The kings speak of her judgment; the merchants speak of her wealth made desolate.

Both laments open with “Woe, woe, the great city” and close “because in one hour.” Revelation 18:19 is spoken by seafarers who grew rich from her, and ends with her being “made desolate” rather than with her judgment.

Jeremiah speaks of Babylon falling “suddenly” and calls for lament, adding that “her judgment reached heaven.” Revelation’s “in one hour thy judgment came” over “Babylon, the mighty city” echoes the sudden fall and the judgment of the same named city.
Both verses present the merchants “weeping and mourning” over her. Revelation 18:15 adds that they “became rich from her” and stand far away for fear of her torment.
Revelation 18:3 introduces “the merchants of the earth” who “became rich from the power of her luxury”; 18:11 shows the same merchants mourning because no one buys their cargo any more.

The cargo list repeats the adornment of the woman in 17:4: “gold and silver and precious stone and pearls … purple … scarlet” corresponds to her being clothed “in purple and scarlet, and adorned with gold and precious stone and pearls.” The city’s trade goods are thus the woman’s own finery.

Both lists of a great trading city’s commerce include trade “in human lives,” and Ezekiel’s Tyre also receives “bronze vessels,” as Babylon’s cargo includes bronze in 18:12. Ezekiel names Greece and its regions as trading partners; Revelation names no partners.
Both pronounce a permanent loss with the same formula: the desired riches “will certainly not” be found “any more,” and Babylon itself “will certainly not be found any more.”
The fruit and splendid things that perished from Babylon correspond to the merchants’ lament in 18:11 that “no one buyeth their cargo any more.”

The merchants adopt the kings’ posture, “standing far away because of the fear of her torment,” and 18:11 already shows “the merchants of the earth weep and mourn over her.” Revelation 18:15 repeats both elements as the merchants’ lament begins.
Revelation 18:3 states that “the merchants of the earth became rich from the power of her luxury”; 18:15 refers back to the same merchants “who became rich from her.”

The city is described in the same terms as the woman in 17:4: “purple and scarlet” and “adorned with gold and precious stone and pearl.” Revelation 18:16 adds “fine linen,” which 17:4 does not mention.
The merchants’ cry “Woe, woe, the great city” repeats the kings’ lament in 18:10. The kings name “Babylon, the mighty city,” while the merchants describe her costly clothing and adornment.

Both verses lament that “in one hour” the city’s wealth was “made desolate,” and both concern those who have ships at sea. Revelation 18:19 adds that the seafarers threw dust on their heads and became rich from her costly wealth.
The seafarers “stood far away” as the kings stand “far away” in 18:10, and both laments turn on judgment or ruin coming “in one hour.”
Isaiah calls on the “ships of Carthage” to wail over the fall of Tyre’s stronghold; Revelation shows helmsmen and sailors standing far away from the fallen city. Isaiah addresses Tyre, not Babylon.

The seafarers see “the smoke of her burning” as the kings do in 18:9, and both groups lament “the great city.” The kings stand far away for fear of her torment; the seafarers cry, “What is like the great city?”

Ezekiel’s mourners over Tyre “raise a cry over you with their voice and cry bitterly” and take up a lament, as the seafarers cry out over the burning city. The Ezekiel text shown does not include a “What is like” question.
Both verses use an acclamation of incomparability: “What is like the great city?” and “Who is like the beast?” The parallel ties the lament for the city to the earlier worship of the beast.
Ezekiel’s mourners over Tyre “cry bitterly” and “put earth on their head,” as the seafarers “threw dust upon their heads and cried.” Both laments are over a maritime trading city.
The merchants’ lament has the same frame as the seafarers’: “Woe, woe, the great city” and “in one hour so great a wealth was made desolate.” Both groups are said to have become rich from her.
Both laments open “Woe, woe, the great city” and close “because in one hour.” In 18:10 the kings speak of her judgment; in 18:19 the seafarers speak of her being made desolate.

The souls under the altar ask how long before the Master will “judge and avenge our blood”; 18:20 announces that “God hath judged your case against her.” Revelation 6:10 names those dwelling on the earth, while 18:20 names her.

The heavenly multitude answers the call to rejoice, praising God because “He judged the great prostitute” and “avenged the blood of His slaves from her hand.” Revelation 18:20 calls heaven to rejoice; 19:1–3 records that rejoicing.

Both verses summon heaven to rejoice: “Rejoice over her, heaven” and “rejoice, heavens and those dwelling in them.” In 12:12 the occasion is the devil’s fall to earth; in 18:20 it is the judgment of the city.

In both passages a stone is thrown into water as a sign of Babylon’s end: Jeremiah binds a stone to a scroll and throws it into the Euphrates, saying “Thus Babylon will sink and certainly not rise.” Revelation’s mighty angel throws a millstone into the sea, saying “In this way Babylon the great city will be thrown.”
The refrain “will certainly not be found any more” in 18:21 continues in 18:22, where craftsmen “will certainly not be found in thee any more” and the sound of a mill is no longer heard.

Ezekiel says of Tyre that God will end “the multitude of your musicians” and that “the sound of your psalteries will certainly no longer be heard,” matching Revelation’s musicians whose sound “will certainly not be heard in thee any more.”

Jeremiah lists sounds removed in judgment, including the sound of joy, “the sound of bridegroom and bride” and “the light of a lamp,” the same items that follow in Revelation 18:22–23. Jeremiah’s list in this reading has “the fragrance of ointment” and no mill.
Isaiah’s judgment says “the lyre’s sound has ceased” along with tambourines, as Revelation silences the lyre players and musicians of the city.

Isaiah says of Tyre, “Her merchants are glorious, rulers of the earth,” and Revelation says “thy merchants were the great ones of the earth.” Isaiah’s oracle concerns Tyre; Revelation applies the description to Babylon.
Nahum’s city is a prostitute and “mistress of potions, selling nations … through her potions,” as Babylon deceived “all the nations” by her sorcery. Nahum addresses Nineveh rather than Babylon.
Both oracles of judgment end “the voice of bridegroom and the voice of bride” in the city. Jeremiah applies this to Judah’s cities and Jerusalem; Revelation applies it to Babylon.
Both verses charge the persecutors with shedding the blood of “saints and prophets.” Revelation 16:6 gives the bowl judgment as repayment; 18:24 locates that blood “in her.”
Jeremiah says “in Babylon wounded men from all the earth will fall,” and Revelation finds in Babylon the blood “of all those slaughtered upon the earth.” Jeremiah does not mention prophets or saints.

The woman is “drunk from the blood of the saints and from the blood of the witnesses of Jesus,” matching the blood of saints found in the city. Revelation 17:18 identifies the woman as the great city.
Both verses report “a voice of a great multitude” crying “Hallelujah.” Revelation 19:6 adds that the voice was like many waters and mighty thunders and praises God’s reign.
A loud voice in heaven proclaims “the salvation and the power” of “our God” in both verses. Revelation 12:10 adds the kingdom and the authority of His Christ; 19:1 adds the glory.

The psalm’s confession “Salvation belongs to the Lord” is echoed in “The salvation … belong to our God.” The psalm speaks of one sufferer’s deliverance; Revelation sets the ascription in heavenly praise.
Both passages speak of avenging “the blood of My slaves” at a woman’s hand: Jezebel’s in 2 Kings, the great prostitute’s in Revelation (“avenged the blood of His slaves from her hand”).
The psalm says “the Lord’s judgments are true, justified together,” as Revelation says “His judgments are true and righteous.”
The martyrs ask God to “judge and avenge our blood”; 19:2 praises Him because He “judged the great prostitute” and “avenged the blood of His slaves.”

Isaiah says of the judged land, “her smoke will rise upward” and it “will not be quenched for an everlasting time”; Revelation says “her smoke goeth up for the ages of the ages.” Isaiah’s oracle is set in Edom’s land, not Babylon.
Both verses describe smoke that “goeth up for ages of ages.” In 14:11 it is the smoke of the torment of the beast’s worshippers; in 19:3 it is the city’s smoke.
The seafarers saw “the smoke of her burning”; the heavenly multitude declares that the same smoke goes up for the ages of the ages.

The four living creatures say “Amen” and the elders fall and worship in both scenes. In 5:14 the worship follows praise of the Lamb; in 19:4 it follows the judgment of the prostitute and adds “Hallelujah.”
The “twenty-four elders” fall and worship God in response to a heavenly announcement in both passages. In 11:16 the announcement is the kingdom of our Lord and His Christ.
The four living creatures and the twenty-four elders fall down together in both verses. In 5:8 they fall before the Lamb with lyres and bowls of incense; in 19:4 they worship God on the throne.
Both verses group God’s “slaves” with “those who fear” Him and add “the small and the great.” In 11:18 they receive their reward; in 19:5 they are called to praise.

The psalm’s summons “Praise the Lord’s name; praise the Lord, slaves” is echoed in “Praise our God, all His slaves.” The psalm opens with “Hallelujah,” the word that frames the surrounding praise in Revelation 19.
The psalm calls “You who fear the Lord, praise Him!”, as Revelation calls “those who fear Him” to praise our God.
Both voices are compared to “the sound of many waters” and to thunder (“great thunder,” “mighty thunders”). In 14:2 the voice is also like lyre players; in 19:6 it is the voice of a great multitude.
The psalm proclaims “The Lord reigned,” and the multitude cries “the Lord God Almighty hath reigned.”
The psalm proclaims “The Lord has become King!” in response to His rule over the peoples, which corresponds to the Hallelujah because God “hath reigned.”
The angel shows John “the bride, the wife of the Lamb,” the wife announced in 19:7 who “prepared herself.”
The new Jerusalem comes down “prepared as a bride adorned for her husband,” matching the announcement that “His wife prepared herself.”

Isaiah pictures the Lord rejoicing over His people as a bridegroom rejoices over a bride; Revelation calls for rejoicing because the marriage of the Lamb has come. Isaiah speaks of the Lord’s joy, Revelation of the worshippers’ joy.

Isaiah’s speaker is clothed by God “in a garment of salvation” and adorned “like a bride,” as the Lamb’s wife is given fine linen to clothe herself. Isaiah’s garment signifies salvation; Revelation’s linen signifies “the righteous acts of the saints.”
The psalm says God’s priests “will clothe themselves in righteousness,” and Revelation explains the bride’s clothing as “the righteous acts of the saints.”

In Ezekiel God clothes Jerusalem, pictured as His bride, and girds her “with fine linen.” Revelation’s bride is likewise given fine linen; Ezekiel’s passage goes on to her unfaithfulness, which Revelation does not.

Jesus’ parable speaks of “those invited to the wedding feast” prepared by a king for his son, as Revelation blesses “those called to the supper of the Lamb’s marriage.” In the parable many of those invited refuse to come.
Both verses contain a beatitude introduced by the command “Write: Blessed are …” In 14:13 the blessed are those who die in the Lord.
Both verses pair the command “Write” with an affirmation of the words: “these words are faithful and true” and “These are true words of God.”

Both verses describe believers “holding the testimony of Jesus.” In 12:17 they are the woman’s offspring whom the dragon attacks; in 19:10 they are John’s brothers, of whom the angel is a fellow slave.
John introduces himself as “your brother” on Patmos because of “the testimony of Jesus,” the same testimony the angel says John and his brothers hold.
Jesus answers Satan with “You shall worship the Lord your God,” and the angel refuses John’s homage with “Worship God.” Both reject worship directed to anyone but God.
The rider is called “Faithful and True,” and in the Laodicean letter Christ is “the faithful and true witness.”

Isaiah’s ruler judges and strikes the earth, and “his loins will be girded with righteousness, and his sides bound with truth.” The rider likewise judges and wages war “in righteousness” and is called “True.”
The psalm says the Lord is coming to judge the world “with righteousness” and the peoples “with His truth.” Revelation’s rider is “True” and judges “in righteousness.”
In the inaugural vision the Son of Man’s eyes are “like a flame of fire,” as the rider’s “eyes are a flame of fire.”

Revelation 2:17–18 has both details: “a new name written, which no one knoweth except the one who receiveth it,” and the Son of God “who hath His eyes like a flame of fire.” In 2:17 the hidden name is given to the one who conquers; in 19:12 it belongs to the rider himself.

Isaiah’s warrior has red garments “as though from a trodden winepress” and brings his enemies’ “blood down to earth,” as the rider wears “a garment dipped in blood.” Revelation 19:15 goes on to describe him treading the winepress.
John’s Gospel calls Christ “the Word,” who was with God and was God; here the rider’s name is “the Word of God.”

Wisdom describes God’s “all-powerful word” leaping from heaven as “a stern warrior” carrying His command “as a sharp sword.” In Revelation the Word of God rides out of heaven to war with a sharp sword from His mouth.
The armies are “clothed in fine linen, white and pure,” as the bride is clothed “in fine linen, bright and pure,” which is explained as the righteous acts of the saints.
In 17:14 the Lamb wages war and conquers, and “those with Him are called and chosen and faithful.” Revelation 19:14 shows those who accompany Him in that war.
Zechariah says “The Lord my God will come, and all the holy ones with Him,” as the heavenly armies follow the rider. Zechariah does not describe horses or garments.
Revelation takes up the psalm’s words “You will shepherd them with an iron rod” for the rider who strikes the nations. The psalm adds “you will crush them like a potter’s vessel.”
In the inaugural vision “from His mouth a sharp two-edged sword was coming out,” as from the rider’s mouth “cometh out a sharp sword.”
Isaiah’s ruler “will strike the earth with the word of his mouth” and slay the ungodly with his breath; the rider strikes the nations with a sword coming from His mouth.
The Lamb is “Lord of lords and King of kings” in 17:14; the rider bears the written name “King of kings and Lord of lords,” with the two titles in reverse order.
Paul calls God “the King of those who reign and Lord of those who rule,” which corresponds to the paired title “King of kings and Lord of lords.”
Nebuchadnezzar confesses Daniel’s God as “God of gods and Lord of kings,” a similar superlative title of sovereignty over kings.

Ezekiel is told to say to “every flying bird … Gather and come!” to God’s great sacrifice, as the angel calls the birds to “gather for the great supper of God.” Ezekiel also summons the beasts of the plain.
The birds summoned to the supper in 19:17 are shown in 19:21 when “all the birds were filled with their flesh.”

Ezekiel’s summons promises the birds “giants’ flesh” and the blood of rulers, and says they will be filled “with horse and rider, giant and every warrior.” Revelation’s list likewise includes “flesh of mighty ones and flesh of horses and of those sitting upon them.”
Both verses list the kings, “commanders of thousands,” the mighty or strong, and both slave and free. In 6:15 they hide from wrath; in 19:18 their flesh is given to the birds.
The ten kings give their authority to the beast and “will wage war with the Lamb.” Revelation 19:19 shows the beast and the kings gathered to wage war with the rider.
Demonic spirits go to “the kings of the whole inhabited world to gather them for the war,” and 19:19 shows the kings and their armies “gathered to wage war.”

Joel summons the nations to “Consecrate war!”, assemble and gather to be judged, and speaks of treading a full winepress. Revelation shows the gathering of kings for war against the rider who treads the winepress (19:15).
Revelation 20:10 says the devil was thrown into “the lake of fire and sulfur, where also are the beast and the false prophet,” referring back to their being thrown there in 19:20.
The false prophet appears with the dragon and the beast, sending spirits “performing signs” to gather the kings, as 19:20 describes him as the one who performed the signs.
Both verses name “the lake burning with fire and sulfur.” Revelation 21:8 assigns it to the unbelieving and other sinners and identifies it as “the second death.”
The sword is that of “the One sitting upon the horse,” from whose mouth “cometh out a sharp sword” to strike the nations in 19:15.
The birds summoned in 19:17–18 to eat the flesh of kings and riders are “filled with their flesh” in 19:21.
In both visions a figure from heaven holds “the key” of the abyss. In 9:1 it is given to a fallen star who opens the shaft; in 20:1 an angel uses it to shut the dragon in.

Jude says God keeps rebellious angels “in everlasting chains under gloom for the judgment,” as the angel comes with “a great chain” to bind the dragon. Jude speaks of angels kept until judgment; Revelation of Satan bound for a thousand years.
Both verses identify “the dragon, the ancient serpent,” as the Devil and Satan. In 12:9 he is thrown down to the earth; in 20:2 he is seized and bound.

Isaiah foresees God bringing His sword against “the dragon, the fleeing serpent,” and killing it, as the angel seizes the dragon, the ancient serpent. Isaiah describes slaying; Revelation here describes binding.
Revelation 20:7–8 fulfils the statement that he “must be loosed”: when the thousand years are completed Satan is loosed from his prison and goes out to deceive the nations.
The angel who has “the key of the abyss” in 20:1 is the one who throws the dragon into the abyss and shuts it.
In 12:9 the serpent is “the one deceiving the whole inhabited world”; 20:3 binds him so that he may “no longer deceive the nations.”

Daniel says the Ancient of Days “gave judgment to the holy ones of the Most High” and they took possession of the kingship, as John sees thrones where “judgment was given to them” and they reign with Christ.
Both verses speak of the souls of those killed “because of the word of God” and because of their testimony. In 6:9 they wait under the altar; in 20:4 they live and reign.

Jesus promises his followers that they will “sit upon twelve thrones, judging” in the regeneration, as John sees those seated on thrones with judgment given to them. Matthew limits the scope to the twelve tribes of Israel.
20:4 says the faithful “lived and reigned with Christ for a thousand years”; 20:5 contrasts “the rest of the dead,” who did not live until the thousand years were completed.
20:5 names this “the first resurrection,” and 20:6 pronounces blessed the one who “hath a share in the first resurrection,” over whom the second death has no authority.
The one who conquers “shall certainly not be harmed by the second death,” as over those in the first resurrection “the second death hath no authority.”
The redeemed are made “a kingdom and priests unto our God,” and “they shall reign”; 20:6 says they will be “priests of God and of Christ” and reign with Him for a thousand years.
Christ has made believers “a kingdom, priests to His God and Father,” anticipating their being “priests of God and of Christ” in 20:6.
Satan is bound “for a thousand years” in 20:2, and 20:7 describes his release “when the thousand years are completed.”
Satan was sealed in the abyss “so that he might no longer deceive the nations until the thousand years were completed”; once loosed, he goes out “to deceive the nations.”
Both verses describe going out to the kings or nations of the world “to gather them for the war.” In 16:14 demonic spirits do the gathering; in 20:8 Satan does.

The foreigners “gathered for war” with people “as numerous as the sand by the sea,” as Satan gathers the nations for war, “whose number is like the sand of the sea.” Samuel narrates a Philistine muster against Israel.
Ezekiel’s Lord says “I will send fire upon Gog,” and in Revelation fire comes down from heaven on the hosts gathered under the name Gog and Magog (20:8).
Ezekiel’s Gog will “come up against My people Israel like a cloud covering the land,” as the nations “came up upon the breadth of the earth” and surrounded the camp of the saints.
