God will “rain fire and sulfur” on Gog and the many nations with him; in Revelation fire from heaven devours the gathered nations, and the devil is then thrown into a lake of fire and sulfur (20:10).
The beast and the false prophet were thrown alive “into the lake of fire burning with sulfur” in 19:20; 20:10 says the devil joins them there.

The beast’s worshippers are “tormented in fire and sulfur,” with no rest “day and night,” their smoke rising “for ages of ages.” Revelation 20:10 uses the same terms of the devil, the beast and the false prophet.
Jesus speaks of “the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels,” and Revelation shows the devil thrown into the lake of fire for the ages of the ages.

Both verses say “nor was a place found for them” / “no place was found for them.” In 12:8 it is the dragon and his angels in heaven; in 20:11 it is the earth and heaven fleeing before the One on the throne.
After earth and heaven flee from the throne, John sees a new heaven and a new earth, “for the first heaven and the first earth passed away.”
Under the seventh bowl “every island fled, and mountains were not found,” as earth and heaven flee and are not found before the throne.
Daniel’s court “sat, and books were opened,” as John sees “scrolls were opened” before the throne for the judgment of the dead.
Revelation 11:18 announces “the time for the dead to be judged” and names “the small and the great”; 20:12 shows the dead, “the great and the small,” judged before the throne.
The Lord gives “each according to his ways and the fruits of his practices,” as the dead are judged “according to their works.”
Both verses say the dead were judged “according to their works”; 20:13 adds that the sea, Death and Hades gave up their dead.
Jesus says all in the tombs will come out, some to “a resurrection of judgment,” according to what they practiced, as the dead are given up and judged by their works.
The risen Christ holds “the keys of death and Hades,” and in 20:13 Death and Hades give up the dead in them.
Both verses identify the lake of fire as “the second death”. Revelation 21:8 assigns a list of evildoers to that lake, whereas here Death and Hades themselves are thrown into it.
Both describe something being “thrown into the lake of fire”. In Revelation 20:10 it is the devil, joining the beast and the false prophet; here it is Death and Hades.
Paul calls death “the last enemy to be brought to nothing”, and Revelation shows Death itself thrown into the lake of fire. Paul does not use the lake-of-fire image.
Revelation 20:12 introduces the scroll “which is of life” and the judgment of the dead. This verse gives the outcome for anyone not found written in “the book of life”.

Both verses describe those judged being thrown into the lake of fire. Revelation 19:20 concerns the beast and the false prophet, “thrown alive”, while this verse concerns anyone not written in the book of life.
Both describe people condemned at the final judgment being sent into fire. Matthew speaks of “the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels”, not of a lake or a book of life.
Isaiah speaks of “the new heaven and new earth that I make”, which matches John’s “a new heaven and a new earth”. Isaiah uses them as a pledge that Israel’s offspring and name will endure.
Isaiah promises that “heaven will be new and earth new” and that former things will not be remembered. John sees this new heaven and earth after the first ones have passed away.

Peter speaks of awaiting, according to God’s promise, “new heavens and a new earth”, and John sees “a new heaven and a new earth”. Peter adds that righteousness dwells there; John adds that the sea is no more.
Both verses name “the new Jerusalem” as coming down out of heaven from God. Revelation 3:12 promises its name to the one who conquers, and here John sees the city itself.
Both describe “the holy city” Jerusalem “coming down out of heaven from God”. Revelation 21:10 adds that John is carried to a great and high mountain to see it.
Isaiah’s speaker says “like a bride He adorned me with ornaments”, and the city comes “prepared as a bride adorned for her husband”. Isaiah applies the image to the rejoicing speaker, not to a city.

Ezekiel’s “My dwelling will be among them. I will be their God, and they will be My people” matches the voice’s announcement that God will dwell with men and that they will be His peoples. Revelation uses the plural “peoples”.
Zechariah joins God’s dwelling in Jerusalem with the formula “They will be My people, and I will be their God”. Revelation joins the same two elements, with God’s tabernacle with men.

Paul quotes God as saying “I will dwell in them and walk among them, and I will be their God, and they will be My people.” Paul applies it to believers as the temple of the living God now, while Revelation announces it at the coming of the new Jerusalem.
Isaiah says death is swallowed and that “God removed every tear from every face”. Revelation joins the same two promises: God will wipe away every tear, and death shall be no more.
Both say that God will wipe every tear from their eyes. In Revelation 7:17 this is said of the multitude shepherded by the Lamb, and here of those with whom God dwells in the new creation.
Isaiah says of those returning to Zion that “Pain, grief and groaning have fled.” Revelation likewise says pain, mourning and crying will be no more. Isaiah’s setting is the return to Zion.
God’s words “Behold, I am doing new things” in Isaiah correspond closely to “Behold, I make all things new.” Isaiah illustrates this with a way in the wilderness and rivers in dry land.
Both verses declare that “these words are faithful and true”. Revelation 22:6 repeats the assurance when the vision closes.
Paul writes that in Christ “the old things passed away; behold, new things have come to be.” Revelation speaks of God making all things new. Paul applies the language to the person who is in Christ.
Both have the self-designation “I am the Alpha and the Omega … the beginning and the end.” Revelation 22:13 also adds “the first and the last”.
Both offer water of life freely to the one who thirsts. In Revelation 22:17 the offer is part of the invitation to come and take, while here God says He will give it.
The title “I am the Alpha and the Omega” is spoken by the Lord God in Revelation 1:8. Here the One on the throne uses it again at the completion of all things.
Both state a filial relationship with God: “you will be sons and daughters to Me” and “he will be My son”. Paul frames it as God being a Father, while Revelation says “I will be his God”.
Revelation 21:3 announces that God will be with His peoples “as their God”. This verse applies the promise to each person who conquers: “I will be his God”.

Both verses contain a promise to “the one who conquereth”, and Revelation 2:11 says that person will not be harmed by the second death. The next verse, 21:8, names the second death as the share of those excluded.
Both list sorcerers, the sexually immoral, murderers, idolaters and those given to falsehood as excluded. Revelation 22:15 places them “outside” the city, while 21:8 assigns them to the lake of fire.
Both mention “the second death”. Revelation 2:11 promises that the one who conquers will not be harmed by it, while this verse gives it as the share of those listed.
Both describe the lake burning with fire and sulfur. In Revelation 19:20 the beast and the false prophet are thrown into it, and here it is the share of the listed evildoers.

Both open with “one of the seven angels having the seven bowls” who spoke with John: “Come, I will show thee”. One shows the judgment of the great prostitute, and the other shows the bride, the wife of the Lamb.
Revelation 19:7 announces the marriage of the Lamb and says “His wife prepared herself”. Here the angel offers to show “the bride, the wife of the Lamb”.

Revelation 21:2 already describes the new Jerusalem as “prepared as a bride adorned for her husband”. Here the angel offers to show the bride, and in the next verse the bride appears as the holy city.
Both describe the holy city Jerusalem “coming down out of heaven from God”. Revelation 21:2 calls it new Jerusalem and compares it to a bride.

Both use the phrase “he carried me away in the Spirit”. In Revelation 17:3 John is taken into a wilderness to see the woman on the scarlet beast, while here he is taken to a great and high mountain to see the holy city.

In Ezekiel a spirit lifts the prophet and brings him “to Jerusalem in a vision of God”. Here John is carried away in the Spirit and shown the holy city Jerusalem. Ezekiel is brought to the existing temple gate rather than shown a city descending.

Ezekiel sees “the glory of the God of Israel” coming, with the earth flashing “like radiance from the glory”. The city likewise has “the glory of God” and a radiance. Ezekiel’s glory comes to the temple by the east gate.
Both use the image of “a jasper stone”. In Revelation 4:3 the One seated on the throne looks like jasper, and here the city’s radiance does.
Revelation 21:23 explains that “the glory of God illuminated” the city, which develops the statement here that it has “the glory of God”.

Ezekiel writes that “The city’s gates will bear the names of Israel’s tribes,” three on each side. Revelation’s city has twelve gates inscribed with the names of the twelve tribes. Ezekiel does not mention angels at the gates.
Revelation 21:17–21 describes the same wall and twelve gates in more detail: the wall’s measure and jasper construction, and gates of pearl.

Both name the tribes “of the sons of Israel”: 7:4–8 counts those sealed “from every tribe of the sons of Israel,” tribe by tribe, while 21:12 inscribes the names of the twelve tribes on the city’s gates.

Ezekiel gives the city three gates facing north, east and south and three toward the sea, each named for a tribe. Revelation gives three gates on each of the four sides. The order differs, and Ezekiel names the western side “toward the sea”.

Paul speaks of believers “built upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets”, and the city’s foundations carry the names of the twelve apostles of the Lamb. Paul also names the prophets and Christ as cornerstone.
Hebrews describes Abraham awaiting “the city that has foundations, whose craftsman and maker is God.” Revelation describes the foundations of the city that comes down from God.
Revelation 21:19–21 continues the description of the same twelve foundations and lists the precious stones that adorn each one.
Both feature a measuring reed. In Revelation 11:1 John is given a reed to measure the temple of God and the altar, while here the angel’s golden reed measures the city, its gates and its wall.
Zechariah sees “a man with a land-measuring cord in his hand”, and here the one speaking with John holds a measuring reed. The verse shown does not state what Zechariah’s figure will measure.
In Ezekiel a guide measures the temple’s doorways and wall in a vision, and here an angel measures the city’s gates and wall. Ezekiel’s measurements concern the temple, not a city.

Both visions end by giving the measurement of the city: Ezekiel’s circuit is “eighteen thousand”, and Revelation’s city is twelve thousand stadia. The figures and units differ, and the verse in Ezekiel does not say the city is foursquare.

Deuteronomy measures Og’s bed “by the cubit of a man”, and Revelation measures the wall in cubits by “a human measure”. Both use the phrase to specify the standard of measure, and Revelation adds that it is also an angel’s.
Both pause to explain a figure. The beast’s number is “a human number”, and the wall’s measure is “a human measure, which is an angel’s”.
Both describe pure gold that is like glass. Here it is the city, “pure gold like pure glass”, and in Revelation 21:21 it is the broad street, “pure gold, like transparent glass”.
The jasper wall echoes the city’s radiance in Revelation 21:11, “like a jasper stone shining as crystal”.

Isaiah promises the city “sapphire as your foundations” and “battlements jasper”, and Revelation names jasper and sapphire as the first two foundations. Isaiah lists fewer stones and assigns jasper to the battlements.

The high priest’s breastpiece has four rows of stones, including sapphire, jasper and emerald, each bearing a name of the twelve tribes. Revelation’s twelve foundations are adorned with stones and bear the apostles’ names. The two stone lists overlap only in part.

Five of the stones named for these foundations also appear in the four rows of stones woven into the priestly fabric in Exodus: “sardius,” “topaz,” “chrysolite,” “beryl” and “amethyst.” The two lists differ in order and in their other stones.
Both compare the city’s gold to glass. Revelation 21:18 says the city is “pure gold like pure glass”, and here the broad street is “pure gold, like transparent glass”.
Revelation 22:2 continues from “its broad street” and places the river and the tree of life in the middle of it.
Babylon, “the great city”, is mourned as adorned with gold and precious stone and pearl. The holy city has gates of pearl and a street of pure gold, so the same materials describe both cities.
Both use the title “Lord God” together with “Almighty”. Revelation 1:8 attaches it to the self-designation “the Alpha and the Omega”, while here the Lord God Almighty is the city’s temple.

John explains that Jesus spoke of “the sanctuary of His body”, and Revelation names the Lamb, with the Lord God Almighty, as the city’s temple. John’s context is the raising of that sanctuary in three days.

Isaiah says the sun and moon will not be the city’s light but “the Lord will be your everlasting light and God your glory.” Revelation says the city needs no sun or moon, for God’s glory illuminates it. Revelation adds that its lamp is the Lamb.
Revelation 22:5 repeats that there is no need of lamplight and sunlight, “because the Lord God will shine upon them.”
Revelation 21:11 first says the city has “the glory of God” with a shining radiance, and this verse names that glory as its light.
Revelation 21:26 restates the same idea, that they will bring “the glory and the honour of the nations” into the city.

Isaiah says Zion will “suck the nations’ milk and eat kings’ wealth”, and Revelation says nations walk by the city’s light and kings bring their glory into it. Isaiah speaks of wealth received rather than glory brought.
Isaiah foresees that “all the nations will come” to the Lord’s mountain and God’s house in the last days. Revelation pictures the nations walking by the light of the city.
Isaiah says “Your gates will be opened continually; day and night they will not be shut”. Revelation says the gates will not be shut by day and that there will be no night.
Revelation 22:5 repeats “night will be no more” and gives the reason that the Lord God will shine upon them.
Zechariah describes a day that is “neither day nor night” with light at evening. Revelation says there will be no night in the city. Zechariah describes a unique day of the Lord rather than a city.
Revelation 21:24 says the kings of the earth bring their glory into the city, and this verse extends it to “the glory and the honour of the nations”.
Isaiah calls Jerusalem “holy city” and says “No uncircumcised and unclean person will pass through you again.” Revelation likewise says nothing common will ever enter the holy city.
Both refer to the book of life belonging to the Lamb. In Revelation 13:8 those not written in it worship the beast, and here only those written in it enter the city.
Both turn on being written in the book of life. In Revelation 20:15 anyone not written is thrown into the lake of fire, and here only those written enter the city.

Both join the throne, the Lamb and waters of life. In Revelation 7:17 the Lamb guides the redeemed to “springs of waters of life”, and here a river of water of life flows from the throne of God and of the Lamb.
Zechariah sees “living water” going out from Jerusalem, and John sees the river of water of life flowing in the city from the throne. Zechariah’s water flows to the first and last seas.
The psalm speaks of a river whose streams “gladden God’s city”. Revelation places a river of water of life in the city of God.

Genesis places “the tree of life in the midst of the garden”, and Revelation places a tree of life in the middle of the city’s street by the river. Revelation adds twelve fruits and leaves for the healing of the nations.
Revelation 2:7 promises the one who conquers to eat from the tree of life in the Paradise of God, and here John sees that tree bearing fruit in the city.
Revelation 22:14 speaks of those who have “right to the tree of life” and enter the city, which refers back to the tree described here.
Zechariah says of Jerusalem “there will no longer be anything accursed”, which closely matches “no accursed thing will be any more.”
Revelation 7:15 says the redeemed are before the throne of God and “serve Him day and night”. Here His slaves serve Him where the throne of God and of the Lamb is.
Both describe the name of God or the Lamb on the foreheads of the faithful. In Revelation 14:1 the hundred forty-four thousand have His name and His Father’s name written there.
Revelation 3:12 promises that the name of God will be written on the one who conquers. Here His name is on the foreheads of His servants.
Jesus promises that the pure in heart “shall see God”, and here His servants “will see His face.” Matthew does not mention a name on the forehead.
Daniel says the holy ones of the Most High will hold the kingdom “for the age of ages”, which closely matches “they will reign for the ages of the ages.”
Daniel says the kingdom is given to a holy people of the Most High “to reign with everlasting kingship”, and here God’s servants reign forever.

The book’s opening and closing both say that God sent His angel to show His slaves “the things that must take place soon.” Revelation 1:1 adds that the revelation was given to Jesus Christ and made known to John.
Both declare that “these words are faithful and true.” In Revelation 21:5 the One on the throne says it, and here the angel repeats it.
Both pronounce a blessing on those who keep “the words of the prophecy” written in this book, at its opening and its close.
Both open with “Behold, I am coming quickly.” Revelation 22:12 adds the promise of reward according to each person’s work.
Both contain the saying “I am coming quickly.” In Revelation 3:11 it comes with the call to hold fast so that no one takes the crown.
Both describe John falling before the angel’s feet to worship. Revelation 19:10 records the same scene earlier in the book, and in both places the angel forbids it.
Revelation 1:1 says the revelation was made known “through His angel to His slave John”. Here John names himself as the one who heard and saw what the angel showed him.

Both have the angel’s rebuke “See that thou do it not! I am thy fellow slave … Worship God.” Revelation 19:10 refers to those holding the testimony of Jesus, and here to the prophets and those keeping the words of this scroll.
Paul warns against those who delight in “worship of angels”, and here the angel refuses John’s worship and directs it to God.
Daniel is told to “seal the book until the time of completion”, while John is told “Do not seal the words of the prophecy of this scroll, for the time is near.”
Daniel’s vision is “closed up, for it is still for many days”, while John’s prophecy is left unsealed because “the time is near.”
Both concern “the words of the prophecy” and give the reason “the time is near”, at the book’s opening and its close.

Daniel says that “many are tested and made holy, and sinners sin”, which Revelation echoes in letting the wrongdoer still do wrong and the holy one still be sanctified. Both appear after the end-time words in Daniel and in Revelation.
Ezekiel’s “Let the one who hears hear, and let the one who disobeys disobey” has the same paired “let … still” form. Ezekiel says it of a rebellious house hearing the prophet.
Isaiah’s “behold, the Lord comes … behold, His reward is with Him” closely matches “Behold, I am coming quickly, and My reward is with Me.”
Jesus says the Son of Man will come and “repay each person according to his conduct”, and Revelation says He comes to repay each according to his work.
Isaiah announces the savior arriving for Zion, “bringing His own reward”. Revelation’s coming One likewise says His reward is with Him.

In Isaiah God says “I am first, and I am after these things; apart from Me there is no God.” Revelation’s “the first and the last” uses the same self-description. In the Septuagint wording Isaiah says “after these things” rather than “last”.
Both use the self-designation “the first and the last.” In Revelation 1:17 the risen One says it to John as he lies at His feet.
Both have “I am the Alpha and the Omega … the beginning and the end.” Here the title is also joined with “the first and the last”.
Both speak of those who wash their robes. Revelation 7:14 adds that they made them white in the blood of the Lamb.
Both promise access to the tree of life. In Revelation 2:7 the promise is to the one who conquers, and here to those who wash their robes.
Revelation 21:27 states who may “enter” the city, those written in the Lamb’s book of life. Here those who wash their robes enter through its gates.
Both list sorcerers, the sexually immoral, murderers, idolaters and those given to falsehood. Revelation 21:8 assigns them to the lake of fire, and here they are “outside”.
Both exclude from the city anyone practicing falsehood. Revelation 21:27 says such people will never enter, and here they are outside.
Revelation 9:20–21 names the unrepented sins of idol worship, murders, sorcerous potions and sexual immorality, the same kinds of sin listed among those outside the city.
Both use the title “the Root of David”. In Revelation 5:5 it is joined with “the Lion from the tribe of Judah”.

Isaiah speaks of a shoot and blossom rising from “the root of Jesse”, and Jesus calls Himself “the Root and the offspring of David”. Both use root imagery for a promised descendant, but Isaiah names Jesse rather than David.
Balaam’s oracle says “A star shall rise from Jacob, and a man shall arise from Israel”, and Jesus calls Himself “the bright morning star”. Numbers does not use the phrase “morning star”.
Both offer water of life freely to the one who thirsts. In Revelation 21:6 God promises to give from its spring, and here the thirsty are invited to come and take.
Jesus cries “If anyone thirsts, let him come to Me and drink”, and Revelation says “let the one who thirsteth come”. Revelation adds the invitation of the Spirit and the bride.

Deuteronomy commands “You shall not add unto the word which I command you, neither shall you take away from it”. Revelation 22:18–19 applies the same warning against adding to or taking from the words of this scroll.
Deuteronomy says of every commanded word “you shall not add unto it, neither shall you take away from it”, and Revelation warns that anyone who adds to its words will receive its plagues.
Proverbs warns “Do not add to His words, so that He may not reprove you”. Revelation warns that God will add plagues to anyone who adds to its words.

Deuteronomy commands “neither shall you take away from it”, and Revelation warns against taking away from the words of this prophecy. Revelation adds the penalty of losing one’s share in the tree of life and the holy city.
The tree of life that a person may lose a share in is the one described in Revelation 22:2.
The “holy city” from which a person’s share may be taken is the one described in Revelation 21:2, coming down out of heaven from God.
Paul’s closing cry “Our Lord, come!” matches the book’s closing response “Come, Lord Jesus.”
Both have the promise “I am coming quickly”. Revelation 22:12 adds that His reward is with Him.
Both have the promise “I am coming quickly”. Revelation 22:7 adds a blessing on those who keep the words of the prophecy.
Both letters close by wishing the grace of the Lord Jesus to be with all: “be with all of you” in 2 Thessalonians and “be with all” here. 2 Thessalonians adds “our” and “Christ”.
Romans has the closing grace wish “The grace of our Lord Jesus be with you”, which is nearly identical to Revelation’s. Revelation extends it to “all”.
